# 1.1 The Emergence of Homo Sapiens and the Neolithic Revolution

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Orienting yourself in time

Before the detail, fix the large landmarks of the period this course covers. Everything in the early chapters happens either before or between these dates.

| Date | Development |
|---|---|
| 3000 BCE | Beginnings of the first civilisations |
| 1000–500 BCE | Assyrians and Persians |
| 400 BCE | Alexander the Great — a short-lived empire; the Romans rule; the Indians are part of the Mauryan Empire |
| Last few centuries BCE | The Qin and Han dynasties of China |

## The emergence of Homo sapiens

**Homo sapiens** originated around 250,000 years ago. Between 200,000 and 150,000 years ago the species settled and developed in Africa, and only around 70,000 years ago did populations move out of Africa. The Neanderthals became extinct around 30,000 BCE.

## The hunter-gatherers of the Palaeolithic Age

**Palaeolithic** means "stone", and the age takes its name from the tools that define it. In Palaeolithic societies both men and women found food; the division of labour that later ages take for granted is not yet in place. Two capacities mark the period out: the use of fire and the use of tools. The age also leaves the first great body of art — paintings of large animals, of which Chauvet is the standard example.

## The Neolithic Revolution

Around 10,000 BCE the end of the ice age led to the **Neolithic Revolution**. *Neolithic* means "new stone", and the name is literal: a new type of polished stone axe appears. The revolution itself, however, is agricultural rather than merely technological. It consists of the growth of crops and the domestication of animals, and because a community that grows its own food no longer needs to follow it, people settled down and populations increased.

Between these two ages sits the **Mesolithic Age**, the "Middle Stone Age", the transition from food gathering to food production.

Systematic agriculture developed between 8000 and 5000 BCE. In the Middle East this meant wheat and barley among crops, and pigs, cattle, goats and sheep among animals. By 4000 BCE agriculture was well developed in central Europe.

## The first towns

Two old towns in the Middle East show what settlement produced. **Jericho** has been occupied since 8000 BCE and was surrounded by mudbrick walls. At **Catal Huyuk** people walked on the rooftops.

Settlement allowed people to build houses, store food and engage in trade. The goods that follow are the physical signature of the Neolithic: pottery, woven baskets, stone tools, and **obsidian**, a volcanic glass that is easily flaked and therefore valuable for tool-making.

Settled agricultural life also led to **patriarchy** — a society dominated by men.

## Invention and the Bronze Age

Between 4000 and 3000 BCE came inventions that greatly changed life: writing, and metal, with bronze appearing in western Asia. The **Bronze Age** runs from 3000 to 1200 BCE.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Homo sapiens** | The human species, originating around 250,000 years ago, settling and developing in Africa 200,000–150,000 years ago and moving out of Africa 70,000 years ago |
| **Palaeolithic** | "Stone"; the age of hunter-gatherers who used fire and tools and painted large animals |
| **Mesolithic Age** | The "Middle Stone Age", the transition from food gathering to food production |
| **Neolithic** | "New stone"; the age of polished stone axes, crop growing and animal domestication |
| **Neolithic Revolution** | The development of agriculture after the end of the ice age around 10,000 BCE, which made people settle down and increased population |
| **Obsidian** | Volcanic glass that is easily flaked |
| **Patriarchy** | Society dominated by men |
| **Bronze Age** | 3000–1200 BCE, following the appearance of metal in western Asia |

# 1.2 The Emergence of Civilisation

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What makes a civilisation

A **civilisation** is a complex culture in which large numbers of people share a variety of common elements. The guide gives seven of them, and it is worth treating the list as a checklist: if you are asked whether a society counts as a civilisation, these are the boxes to tick.

| # | Element |
|---|---|
| 1 | An urban focus |
| 2 | Political and military structures |
| 3 | A social structure based on economy |
| 4 | Complexity in material life — agriculture, trade, luxury items |
| 5 | Religion |
| 6 | Writing |
| 7 | Artistic and intellectual activity |

## Early civilisations around the world

The first civilisations are not confined to one region, and they do not all appear at once. Three examples fix the spread.

| Civilisation | Date |
|---|---|
| Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro | 3000–1500 BCE |
| The Shang dynasty in China | 1570–1045 BCE |
| The city of Caral, Peru | 2600 BCE |

## Why did early civilisations develop?

Two causes are given, and they answer different halves of the question.

The first is economic. A **food surplus** — more food than the producers themselves need — frees people from producing food, and that leads to **job specialisation**. This is the material precondition for several of the seven elements above: without specialists there are no full-time priests, soldiers, scribes or artists.

The second is religion, which provides unity among humans. Where surplus makes a complex society possible, religion is what holds that complex society together.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Civilisation** | A complex culture in which large numbers of people share a variety of common elements: urban focus, political/military structures, a social structure based on economy, complexity in material life, religion, writing, and artistic/intellectual activity |
| **Food surplus** | Surplus food production, which leads to job specialisation |
| **Job specialisation** | The division of work into distinct occupations, made possible by a food surplus |

# 1.3 Civilisation in Mesopotamia

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The land

**Mesopotamia** is the valley between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. Its agriculture depended on irrigation and on the control of the river flow, so the management of water is the practical foundation of everything that follows: the cities, the priesthoods and the kings all rest on a river that has to be harnessed.

## The city-states of ancient Mesopotamia

The **Sumerians** were the first Mesopotamian civilisation. By 3000 BCE there were independent cities, of which Ur is the standard example. Walls surrounded the cities and dwellings were built of sun-dried brick.

At the centre of each city stood a **ziggurat**, a temple dedicated to the chief god or goddess, built atop a massive tower. The priest or priestess held political power, and Sumerian government was therefore a **theocracy** — government by divine authority — in which the king was an agent from God.

## Empires in ancient Mesopotamia

The city-states did not stay independent. Two empires follow.

The **Akkadians** lived north of the Sumerians and were a Semitic people. In 2340 BCE **Sargon**, leader of the Akkadians, overthrew the Sumerians. Akkadian power was based on the military, and an attack from a neighbour brought the empire to an end.

**Hammurabi's empire**, centred on Babylon, begins in 1792 BCE. Hammurabi was known as the "Sun of Babylon". The empire fell after his death, but he is remembered above all for **Hammurabi's Code**.

## The culture of Mesopotamia

The great literary survival is the **Epic of Gilgamesh**, about the legendary king of Uruk. Mesopotamian religion was **polytheistic**, and it included **divination**: relieving anxiety by finding out the gods' intentions.

From 3000 BCE the Sumerians used the **cuneiform** system of writing. They were also strong in mathematics and astronomy.

## An exam note

Section 1.4 will not be tested.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Mesopotamia** | The valley between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers |
| **Sumerians** | The first Mesopotamian civilisation, with independent walled cities such as Ur by 3000 BCE |
| **Ziggurat** | A temple dedicated to the chief god or goddess, built atop a massive tower |
| **Theocracy** | Government by divine authority, with the king as an agent from God |
| **Sargon** | Leader of the Akkadians who overthrew Sumerian power in 2340 BCE |
| **Hammurabi** | Ruler of Babylon from 1792 BCE, the "Sun of Babylon", author of Hammurabi's Code |
| **Epic of Gilgamesh** | The Mesopotamian epic about the legendary king of Uruk |
| **Divination** | Relieving anxiety by finding out the gods' intentions |
| **Cuneiform** | The writing system used by the Sumerians from 3000 BCE |

# 1.5 New Centres of Civilisation

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Nomadic peoples: the impact of the Indo-Europeans

### The Hittites

From around 1750 BCE the **Hittites** were established in Asia Minor, or Anatolia. Their distinguishing technology was iron, and they transformed Mesopotamian cultures. The Hittite state ends in 1190 BCE.

### The Phoenicians

The Phoenicians are remembered for one thing above all: the invention of the alphabet. Politically they were defeated by the Assyrians and then the Persians, but the alphabet outlived them and, as a later section shows, passed through the Greeks to much of the world.

## The Hebrews

The Hebrews were the "Children of Israel", and their defining religious feature is **monotheism**. They moved to Egypt, where they were enslaved by the pharaohs.

### The kings

| Ruler | Achievement |
|---|---|
| Saul | The beginning of the united kingdom of Israel; after his death, anarchy |
| David | Saul's lieutenant; established control over all of Canaan |
| Solomon | David's son; strengthened royal power |

### The Kingdom of Judah

Judah was forced to pay tribute to Assyria and gained independence only after Assyria's decline. That independence did not last: the **Chaldeans** defeated Assyria and then conquered Judah. In 586 BCE Jerusalem was destroyed and the upper class was taken to Babylon for captivity. When the Persians destroyed the Chaldeans, the Jews were allowed to come back. Judah then remained under Persian control until Alexander the Great.

### Hebrew religion

Three ideas structure it:

- **The Covenant**, between Yahweh and the people
- **The Law**, that is, obedience to God
- **The prophets**

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Hittites** | An Indo-European people in Asia Minor/Anatolia from 1750 BCE who made use of iron and transformed Mesopotamian cultures; ended 1190 BCE |
| **Phoenicians** | The people credited with the invention of the alphabet, later defeated by the Assyrians and Persians |
| **Monotheism** | Belief in one God, the defining feature of Hebrew religion |
| **Chaldeans** | The people who defeated Assyria and conquered Judah, destroying Jerusalem in 586 BCE |
| **The Covenant** | The agreement between Yahweh and the people |
| **The Law** | Obedience to God |

# 1.6 The Rise of New Empires

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The Assyrian Empire

The Assyrians emerged in Assyria, on the Upper Tigris, and were Semitic-speaking. Under **Ashurbanipal** the empire was overextended; by his reign Babylon was in rebellion and Assyria began to disintegrate. Overextension is the point to hold on to — the same military reach that built the empire is what made it impossible to hold.

Assyrian power rested on terror and warfare, which produced excellence in the military. Religion was the cohesive force in society. Ethnicity was not important; language was the marker of identity. The empire also lived on trade and agriculture, and it assimilated much of Sumerian and Babylonian culture.

## The Persian Empire

### Neo-Babylon

In 539 BCE the Neo-Babylonian state falls. **Nebuchadnezzar** had rebuilt Babylon after its collapse.

### The rise of Persia

The Persians came from southwestern Iran, and the **Achaemenid** dynasty unified them.

| Ruler | Achievement |
|---|---|
| Cyrus the Great | From 550 BCE extended Persian control over the Medes |
| Cambyses | Cyrus's son; invaded Egypt |
| Darius | Built the largest empire the world had ever seen |

### Governing the empire

The Medes became the first **satrapy**, or province, and Babylonia was likewise made into a province under a **satrap**, or governor. Existing government officials kept their positions — a policy that explains how so large an empire could be absorbed so quickly, since conquest did not require rebuilding local administration from nothing.

### Zoroastrianism

From around 660 BCE **Zoroaster** taught a monotheistic religion whose God is **Ahuramazda**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Ashurbanipal** | Assyrian ruler by whose reign the empire was overextended, Babylon rebelled and Assyria disintegrated |
| **Nebuchadnezzar** | Ruler who rebuilt Babylon after its collapse |
| **Achaemenid dynasty** | The dynasty that unified the Persians of southwestern Iran |
| **Cyrus the Great** | Persian ruler who from 550 BCE extended Persian control over the Medes |
| **Satrapy** | A province of the Persian Empire; the Medes were the first |
| **Satrap** | The governor of a satrapy |
| **Darius** | Persian ruler who built the largest empire the world had ever seen |
| **Zoroastrianism** | The monotheistic religion taught by Zoroaster from around 660 BCE, whose God is Ahuramazda |

# 2.1 Classical Greece

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Geography decides politics

Greek geography dictated many of the decisions and characteristics of Greek civilisation. The terrain is mountainous, with no fertile land for agriculture, so the Greeks relied on trade. Distance and mountains also made some areas hard to control, and that difficulty shaped politics directly: it is why Greece produced independent city-states rather than a single unified kingdom.

## Daily life

### Gender roles

Men worked as artisans, farmers and merchants in the morning, and in the afternoon exercised and attended assemblies. Women cooked and wove at home; poorer women worked in the markets, selling food and cloth.

The upper class attended **symposiums**, where public affairs, philosophy and literature were discussed. Entertainment at them included dancers, singers, magicians, acrobats and alcohol.

### Slavery

Around one third of the population was enslaved. The enslaved were prisoners of war, foreigners and debtors. They did heavy work and mining, though some were teachers or servants.

## Athens

Athens began as an aristocracy.

### Education

The sons of free men were required to be educated. The main texts were the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey*, and the curriculum covered arithmetic, geometry, drawing, music, gymnastics and rhetoric. At eighteen they were required to serve in the military for two years.

### Architecture and the arts

Greek builders started using stone around the sixth century BCE; before that wood was the main material. The guide distinguishes three column types: **Ionic** (flat tops), **Doric** (curly tops) and **Corinthian** (very fancy).

Sculptors used idealised forms. **Phidias** created the statues for the Parthenon and the statue of Zeus at Olympus.

### Reform: why Athens changed

Athens had many social problems that forced change — above all poverty and debt. The three reformers below are best read as a sequence, each one finishing what the last began.

**Draco and the archons.** An **archon** was the leader of the aristocratic government and the supreme judge. Draco created a strict code of law to curb crimes, so strict that the word **draconian** now means excessively harsh or severe, especially of laws or their application. He also extended voting rights to anyone with armour.

**Solon**, elected archon in 594 BCE, continued solving the problems Draco had tried to solve. He cancelled or reduced debts and eliminated slavery for debt, and he eliminated the "helot" class except for foreigners and women.

**Cleisthenes** finished what the previous archons had started, and his reforms were the ones that empowered common people. He redesigned the electoral districts so that they were not divided by wealth, and he created the **Council of Five Hundred**: five hundred people chosen by chance to help run the government. Because places were allotted rather than elected, most people could participate at least once, and any free man could now become powerful.

He also began **ostracism**: if six thousand people wrote someone's name on an **ostrakon**, a piece of broken pottery, that person was banished for ten years. Finally he expanded the Court of Appeal juries, with 1,501 jurors sitting at once — a number large enough to protect against corruption.

## Influences on and of Greece

Greece both borrowed and lent. The civilisations of the Near East and Egypt influenced Greek culture. In the other direction, Greek religion and its features were adopted into Roman culture, and the Greek alphabet — which itself came from the Phoenicians — was adopted by many other civilisations.

## Sparta

Sparta was founded by the descendants of the Dorians, who invaded Greece around 1200 BCE, and was located on the Peloponnesus. It invaded its neighbours and enslaved many of them, so that between 65 and 85 per cent of the population were enslaved **helots**, who farmed the large estates. **Citizen** in Sparta meant the land-owning leisure class: by definition, citizens owned helots and did not have to work.

Education began at around seven years old, in a military camp for boys with no weapons or armour, designed to create faithful citizens.

### Gender roles

Spartan women had more freedom than other Greek women but had no place in government. They were expected to exercise and be strong so as to give birth to strong babies.

### Government

| Body | Composition and role |
|---|---|
| The two kings | Little power, almost figureheads; led the army and religious services |
| The assembly | Males over thirty; held the most power |
| The council of elders | Twenty-eight men over sixty; similar to a supreme court |

### The limits of Sparta

Despite Sparta's popularity and its reputation as an advanced state with an all-powerful army, it was behind on the arts, science and similar fields, and was very conservative. The reason is given plainly: the Spartans were afraid of change and of outside influence.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Symposium** | A gathering of the upper class at which public affairs, philosophy and literature were discussed |
| **Archon** | The leader of the aristocratic government and supreme judge |
| **Draconian** | Excessively harsh or severe, especially of laws or their application |
| **Council of Five Hundred** | Cleisthenes' body of five hundred people chosen by chance to help run the government |
| **Ostracism** | Banishment for ten years if six thousand people wrote a person's name on an ostrakon |
| **Ostrakon** | A piece of broken pottery used for writing a name in an ostracism vote |
| **Helot** | An enslaved farm worker in Sparta, making up 65–85 per cent of the population |
| **Citizen (Sparta)** | The land-owning leisure class, who owned helots and did not have to work |
| **Phidias** | Sculptor who created the statues for the Parthenon and the statue of Zeus at Olympus |

# 2.2 The Founding of Rome and the Roman Republic

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Origin myths

Rome told two stories about its own beginning.

**Aeneas** was the son of the goddess Venus and a mortal man, a Trojan hero fighting for the Greeks, who founded Rome.

**Romulus and Remus** were the twin sons of Mars. The boys were set adrift on the Tiber, found by a she-wolf and then raised by a shepherd's family. Romulus killed Remus.

## The Roman conquest of Italy

At the beginning of the Republic, Rome was surrounded by enemies, including the Latin communities. The conquest of Italy runs as follows.

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 338 BCE | Rome crushed the Latin states in Latium |
| The next fifty years | Successful struggles with the hill people of central Italy, then direct contact with the Greek communities |
| 267 BCE | Rome completed the conquest of southern Italy by defeating the Greek cities |
| 264 BCE | Rome crushed the Etruscan states in the north and had conquered most of Italy |

In 338 BCE the Romans also devised the **Roman Confederation**. Some people, the Latins, were given full Roman citizenship; the remaining communities were made allies. Allies were free to run their local affairs but were required to provide soldiers for Rome, and loyal allies could improve their status and even become Roman citizens. The arrangement therefore turned conquest into recruitment: every victory enlarged the pool of soldiers available for the next one.

## The Roman state

After the overthrow of the monarchy, Roman nobles were eager to maintain their position of power, and established a republican form of government.

### Magistrates

**Consuls** and **praetors** were the chief executive officers of the Roman Republic. Two consuls were chosen annually; they administered the government and led the army into battle. The office of praetor was created in 336 BCE and was in charge of civil law, but a praetor could also lead armies and govern Rome when the consuls were away.

### Senate and assemblies

The **Roman Senate** came to hold an especially important position. Formally it could only advise the magistrates, but this advice was not taken lightly, and by the third century BCE it had virtually the force of law.

The **Centuriate Assembly** elected the chief magistrates and passed laws. Its structure mattered more than its function: the wealthiest citizens always had a majority in it.

The **Council of the Plebs** came into being in 471 BCE.

## Social divisions

| | Patricians | Plebeians |
|---|---|---|
| Who they were | Descendants of the original senators appointed during the period of the kings; great landowners; an aristocratic governing class | The larger group of non-patrician landowners, less wealthy landholders, artisans, merchants and small farmers |
| Citizenship | Citizens | Citizens |
| Voting | Could vote | Could vote |
| Office | Only they could be consuls, magistrates and senators; controlled the centuriate assembly | Could not hold governmental office |

Intermarriage between the two orders was forbidden.

## The struggle of the orders

In the fifth century BCE the plebeians began to seek equality, and won it in stages.

- The **Council of the Plebs**, a popular assembly for plebeians only, was created in 471 BCE.
- The **tribunes of the plebs** were given power to protect plebeians against arrest by patrician magistrates.
- Intermarriage was allowed.
- In 287 BCE the plebeians could pass laws.

The outcome was not the levelling that might be expected. Because intermarriage was now permitted, a select number of patrician and plebeian families formed a new senatorial aristocracy that came to dominate the political offices. The struggle of the orders replaced one narrow governing class with another.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Aeneas** | Son of the goddess Venus and a mortal man; a Trojan hero fighting for the Greeks who founded Rome |
| **Romulus and Remus** | Twin sons of Mars, set adrift on the Tiber, found by a she-wolf and raised by a shepherd's family; Romulus killed Remus |
| **Roman Confederation** | The 338 BCE arrangement giving some Latins full Roman citizenship and making the remaining communities allies who ran their own affairs but supplied soldiers |
| **Consuls** | Two chief executive officers chosen annually who administered the government and led the army |
| **Praetor** | Office created in 336 BCE, in charge of civil law, able also to lead armies and govern Rome in the consuls' absence |
| **Roman Senate** | Body that could only advise the magistrates but whose advice had virtually the force of law by the third century BCE |
| **Centuriate Assembly** | Assembly in which the wealthiest citizens always had a majority; elected chief magistrates and passed laws |
| **Patricians** | Descendants of the original senators; great landowners and the aristocratic governing class |
| **Plebeians** | The larger group of non-patrician landowners, artisans, merchants and small farmers |
| **Council of the Plebs** | Popular assembly for plebeians only, created in 471 BCE |
| **Tribunes of the plebs** | Officers given power to protect plebeians against arrest by patrician magistrates |

markdown:
# 2.3 The Roman Conquest of the Mediterranean

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Carthage

Carthage was founded around 800 BCE on the coast of North Africa by the Phoenicians, and flourished. By the third century BCE it held northern Africa, southern Spain, Sardinia, Corsica and western Sicily, and controlled western Mediterranean trade. It was therefore not a distant rival but the power that owned the sea Rome had just reached.

## The Punic Wars

### The First Punic War (264–146 BCE)

The Romans decided to intervene in a struggle between two Sicilian cities and sent an army to Sicily. The Carthaginians considered Sicily part of their territory, so war began. To fight a naval power the Romans developed a navy. Carthage gave up all rights to Sicily, and Sicily became the first Roman province; Corsica, Sardinia and Sicily all became part of Rome.

Afterwards the Carthaginian general **Hannibal Barca** swore to restore his nation's honour.

### The Second Punic War (218–201 BCE)

The Romans encouraged one of Carthage's Spanish allies to revolt against Carthage. Hannibal crossed the Alps with an army of thirty to forty thousand men and terrorised the Romans for fifteen years. At the **Battle of Cannae** in 216 BCE the Romans lost 400,000 men and were on the brink of disaster.

Rome recovered by changing method rather than by winning a bigger battle.

- The Romans began to reconquer the Italian cities that had gone over to Hannibal's side.
- **Fabius Maximus**, as dictator, avoided pitched battles and attacked supply lines — the **Fabian strategy**.
- **Scipio Africanus the Elder** learned from Hannibal's own tactics and pushed the Carthaginians out of Spain by 206 BCE.
- The Romans then took the war directly to Carthage, forcing the Carthaginians to recall Hannibal from Italy.

At the **Battle of Zama** in 202 BCE the Romans crushed Hannibal's forces and Carthage lost Spain. Rome became the dominant power in the western Mediterranean.

### The Third Punic War (149–146 BCE)

In 146 BCE Carthage was destroyed. It burned for ten days, fifty thousand people in the area were sold into slavery, and Carthage became a Roman province called Africa.

## The nature of Roman imperialism

Roman expansion is best divided into three stages:

1. The conquest of Italy
2. The conflict with Carthage and expansion into the western Mediterranean
3. Involvement with, and domination of, the Hellenistic kingdoms

## The Roman army

The army was built of four legions, each made up of four to five thousand men. Each legion had about three hundred cavalry, and the rest was infantry. Soldiers were recruited from citizens between eighteen and forty-six.

The terms of service changed over time, and the change matters for what comes later. At first soldiers were unpaid, provided their own weapons and could join if they wanted — service rested on loyalty. Later they received professional training and a stipend. Later still they received the spoils of victory.

## Other wars

| War | Dates | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Jugurthine Wars | 112–106 BCE | Sulla and Marius add parts of Africa to Rome |
| Social War | 91–87 BCE | Italian cities revolt, desiring citizenship, since the Roman military relied heavily on their populations |
| Mithridatic War | 88–63 BCE | Sulla and Pompey add much of Anatolia to Rome |
| Three Servile Wars | 135–132, 104–100, 73–71 BCE | Slave rebellions in Sicily and southern Italy, including Spartacus |

## The results of conquest

Conquest made Rome rich and destabilised it at the same time.

The gap between rich and poor widened. More land meant that patricians could buy more land at a cheaper price and acquire slaves to work it, while plebeians got less land and moved to the cities unemployed. Country life changed accordingly, dominated by the **latifundia**, massive farming estates worked by many slaves, sustained by an influx of enslaved people.

Culturally, a new Hellenised urban culture appeared: Roman literature mimicked Greek modes and Romans adopted Greek-style baths. There were greater opportunities for Roman aristocrats, politically and materially.

There was also a cost that is easy to miss: the loss of enemies meant the loss of patriotism and of Roman frugality.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Carthage** | City founded around 800 BCE by the Phoenicians on the North African coast, controlling western Mediterranean trade by the third century BCE |
| **Hannibal Barca** | Carthaginian general who swore to restore national honour and crossed the Alps with 30,000–40,000 men |
| **Battle of Cannae** | 216 BCE battle in which the Romans lost 400,000 men and were on the brink of disaster |
| **Fabian strategy** | Fabius Maximus's method of avoiding pitched battles and attacking supply lines |
| **Scipio Africanus the Elder** | General who learned from Hannibal's tactics and pushed the Carthaginians out of Spain by 206 BCE |
| **Battle of Zama** | 202 BCE battle in which the Romans crushed Hannibal's forces; Carthage lost Spain |
| **Legion** | Roman army unit of 4,000–5,000 men, about 300 of them cavalry and the rest infantry |
| **Latifundia** | Massive farming estates worked by many slaves |

# 2.4 The Decline and Fall of the Roman Republic

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The period runs from 133 to 31 BCE.

## Growing inequality and unrest

By the second century BCE the Senate had become the effective governing body of the Roman state. It was three hundred men drawn primarily from the landed aristocracy; they remained senators for life and held the chief magistracies of the Republic.

The backbone of the Roman state and army had traditionally been the small farmers, but over time the small farmers could not compete for land. Aristocrats amassed large estates, the **latifundia**, worked by slave labour. This is the structural crisis behind everything that follows: the class that filled the legions was being squeezed out of existence.

### The Gracchi

**Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus** were two brothers who tried to remedy this growing economic and social crisis. They believed the underlying cause of Rome's problems was the decline of the small farmer. They demanded land redistribution and wanted the government to buy food for the poor.

Senators murdered Tiberius in 133 BCE. Gaius was murdered twelve years later.

## A new role for the Roman army

**Gaius Marius** (157–86 BCE) held the consulship from 104 to 100 BCE. He recruited volunteers from both the urban and the rural poor who possessed no property. These men swore an oath of loyalty to the general, not to Rome.

The consequence follows directly. Generals would promise their soldiers land, which forced the generals to play politics in order to get laws passed that would provide the land promised. Marius therefore created a system that placed much power in the hands of individual generals instead of the state.

### Sulla

The Senate gave **Lucius Cornelius Sulla** command of a war in Asia Minor, but when the council of the plebs tried to transfer command of this war to Marius, civil war broke out. Sulla won and seized Rome in 82 BCE. He was declared dictator, marched on Rome and in 81 BCE slaughtered thousands because of his disagreements with Marius.

## The collapse of the Republic

Two features define the collapse: the jostling for dominance of a number of powerful individuals, and the civil wars generated by their conflict.

| Man | Base of power |
|---|---|
| Crassus | The richest man in Rome; led a successful military command against a major slave rebellion; command in Syria |
| Pompey | Returned from a successful military command in Spain in 71 BCE, hailed as a military hero |
| Julius Caesar | Military command in Spain; a special military command in Gaul, modern France |

The three formed a coalition that historians call the **First Triumvirate**, or three-man rule. Crassus died in battle in 53 BCE, leaving Caesar and Pompey in direct competition.

Leading senators endorsed Pompey as less harmful to their cause and voted for Caesar to lay down his command and return as a private citizen. Caesar refused, kept his army and moved into Italy illegally by crossing the Rubicon, then marched on Rome and defeated Pompey and his allies.

### Caesar

Caesar was made dictator in 47 BCE, and three years later dictator for life. His measures were:

- Public works to reduce unemployment
- Public land given to the poor
- Expanded citizenship
- The Julian calendar

He also planned many building projects and military adventures in the east. In 44 BCE a group of leading senators assassinated him.

## The Second Triumvirate

After Caesar's death, power passed to Octavian, Antony and Lepidus.

**Octavian** was Caesar's grandnephew and adopted son, and took the western portion. **Antony**, Caesar's ally and assistant, took the eastern half and allied himself closely with the Egyptian queen Cleopatra VII, although he was originally married to Octavian's sister Octavia. Octavian crushed Antony's forces at the **Battle of Actium** in Greece.

## Augustus

In 27 BCE Octavian proclaimed himself emperor and proclaimed the restoration of the Republic — the two claims were made together, and the contradiction is the point. The Senate gave him the title **Imperator**, commander in chief, the Latin origin of "emperor". Many people believed Caesar had been a tyrant, whereas Augustus was careful to present himself as an ordinary citizen.

His position rested on both force and form. He maintained an army of twenty-eight legions, some 150,000 men, and set up the **Praetorian Guard** of roughly nine thousand men with the important task of guarding the emperor. He was made consul for life and held the power to veto, to make laws and to call the Senate, while maintaining the facade of elected officials rather than dictators.

## The legacy of the Roman Republic

- The spread of Greco-Roman culture
- Roman law, including *jus naturale*, universal or natural law. Roman law was harmonised with the needs of a global empire and guided mostly by reason and logic
- Infrastructure: well-built military roads radiating from Rome, and roads for civil use
- Military ability, and the strategy of divide and control
- The treatment of conquered peoples

The guide leaves one question deliberately open, and it is worth being ready for it: when did the Roman Republic end?

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Latifundia** | Large estates amassed by aristocrats and worked by slave labour |
| **Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus** | Brothers who demanded land redistribution and state food purchases for the poor; both murdered |
| **Gaius Marius** | Consul 104–100 BCE who recruited propertyless volunteers who swore loyalty to the general rather than to Rome |
| **First Triumvirate** | The three-man coalition of Crassus, Pompey and Julius Caesar |
| **Second Triumvirate** | The three-man rule of Octavian, Antony and Lepidus after Caesar's death |
| **Battle of Actium** | The battle in Greece at which Octavian crushed Antony's forces |
| **Imperator** | "Commander in chief", the title given to Augustus by the Senate; Latin for "emperor" |
| **Praetorian Guard** | Force of roughly 9,000 men set up by Augustus to guard the emperor |
| **Jus naturale** | Universal, natural law |

# 2.5 The Early Roman Empire and the Origins of Christianity

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The origins of Christianity

Christianity begins between 30 BCE and 1 CE with a Jew named **Jesus** in Judea, that is, Israel. He was born in Nazareth in the twenty-third year of Augustus, and raised in Galilee. He was born to a virgin mother, Mary, and God is his father.

Jesus travelled and preached in Judea — Bethlehem, Nazareth, Galilee and Jerusalem — and performed miracles. His popularity became threatening to Roman leaders, and he was crucified for it. He then rose from the dead three days later and ascended to heaven.

The **apostles** spread the message and wrote the four Gospels on the life of Jesus in the New Testament.

## Beliefs

- Monotheism, but Trinitarian: the **Holy Trinity**, in which Father, Son and Spirit are each God
- Jesus is the **Messiah**
- **Salvation**: people can be forgiven from sin and achieve eternal life in heaven, or go to hell
- Jesus will come again

## Scripture

The scripture is the Bible, which contains two parts:

| Part | Contents |
|---|---|
| Old Testament | The Jewish Torah |
| New Testament | Stories of Jesus and the early Christians |

## The Julio-Claudian dynasty and the Pax Romana

Augustus wanted his stepson **Tiberius** to be his successor, and so established the **Julio-Claudian dynasty**. The period that follows is the **Pax Romana**, and the **Five Good Emperors** rule from 96 to 180.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Jesus** | A Jew of Judea, born in Nazareth in the twenty-third year of Augustus and raised in Galilee, with whom Christianity begins |
| **Apostles** | Those who spread Jesus's message and wrote the four Gospels of the New Testament |
| **Holy Trinity** | The Christian doctrine that Father, Son and Spirit are each God, within a monotheistic faith |
| **Messiah** | The title Christians give to Jesus |
| **Salvation** | Forgiveness from sin and eternal life in heaven, as against hell |
| **Julio-Claudian dynasty** | The dynasty established by Augustus, who wanted his stepson Tiberius to succeed him |
| **Pax Romana** | The period of Roman peace, including the Five Good Emperors (96–180) |

# 7.1 Muhammad and the Rise of Islam

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Arabia before Islam

The **Arabs** are a Semitic-speaking people of southwestern Asia with a long history. The **Bedouin Arabs** were nomadic peoples who came originally from the northern part of the peninsula. They lived by sheepherding and by raiding passing caravans, but the domestication of the camel changed that: once camels could carry goods across the desert, the Bedouin began to trade.

**Mecca** was a centre of commerce and trade, and hosted many travellers and nomads. The region as a whole was politically fragmented and religiously diverse.

## Muhammad

**Muhammad** was born in Mecca in 570 CE. He married a wealthy widow, **Khadijah**. In 610 CE he received his first revelation from God, and began to practise a monotheistic religion of submission to God. His spiritual visions unified the Arab world.

He gained followers in Mecca, but also met resistance there, and in 622 the leaders of Mecca drove him out. His flight to Medina in 622 CE is the **Hegira**, and in Medina he established the first Muslim community, the **umma**.

## Core beliefs

Islam is a monotheistic faith recognising **Allah** as the sole deity and Muhammad as his Prophet.

## The major texts

| Text | What it is |
|---|---|
| The Quran | The scripture |
| The Tafsir | Exegesis of the Quran |
| The Hadith | The collected sayings of Muhammad |
| The Sira | The biography of Muhammad |

## The Five Pillars of Islam

The pillars can be remembered by the initials **CPFCP**.

| Pillar | Practice |
|---|---|
| C | Confession of faith — belief in Allah and Muhammad |
| P | Pray, facing Mecca, five times a day |
| F | Fast, during Ramadan |
| C | Charity, the day of Zakat |
| P | Pilgrimage, the hajj, to Mecca to worship the Ka'ba at least once in a lifetime |

## Shari'a and a way of life

After Muhammad's death, scholars developed the **Shari'a**, a comprehensive legal code. Islam is therefore not confined to worship: it emphasises behaviour as well as belief, and integrates spiritual and societal duties as guided by the Qur'an and Shari'a law.

## Historical and textual considerations

Historical accounts of Muhammad's life are speculative and rely on sources such as the Qur'an and the Hadith. This is worth stating plainly, because the same sources serve as both religious scripture and historical evidence.

## Impact

Islam rapidly transformed Arabian society and united the region under a single religious and political framework — a single framework, not two, which is why the succession crisis after Muhammad's death was simultaneously a religious and a political problem.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Arabs** | Semitic-speaking people of southwestern Asia with a long history |
| **Bedouin Arabs** | Nomadic peoples originally from the northern part of the peninsula, who lived by sheepherding and raiding caravans and began to trade after the domestication of camels |
| **Mecca** | A centre of commerce and trade that hosted many travellers and nomads; Muhammad's birthplace |
| **Khadijah** | The wealthy widow Muhammad married |
| **Hegira** | Muhammad's flight from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE |
| **Umma** | The first Muslim community, established at Medina |
| **Allah** | The sole deity recognised by Islam, with Muhammad as his Prophet |
| **The Quran** | The scripture of Islam |
| **The Tafsir** | Exegesis of the Quran |
| **The Hadith** | The collected sayings of Muhammad |
| **The Sira** | The biography of Muhammad |
| **Shari'a** | The comprehensive legal code developed by scholars after Muhammad's death |

# 7.2 The Caliphate and the Sunni–Shi'a Split

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The succession crisis

Muhammad died in 632 CE and left no male heir and no named successor, which created a leadership crisis. There were two candidates for **caliph**, an office that was at once political and religious.

| Candidate | Relationship to Muhammad | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Ali | Cousin and son-in-law | Deemed too young |
| Abu Bakr | Father-in-law and close friend | Chosen; caliph 632–634 |

Abu Bakr continued working part time to make a living, loosely controlled his warriors, and united all the Arab tribes.

## The road to the split

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 656 | The third caliph, Uthman, is murdered; Ali is supported and named caliph |
| 657 | War erupts between Uthman's supporters and Ali's supporters |
| 660 | The Umayyads declare their own caliph in Jerusalem |
| 661 | Ali is assassinated, and his son is killed in battle |

## The two positions

The divide that opened in 632 and hardened by 661 has never closed, and the disagreement is specifically about who may legitimately succeed Muhammad.

| | Sunni | Shi'a |
|---|---|---|
| Share of Muslims | 85 per cent | 15 per cent |
| Core claim | Muhammad cannot be succeeded as prophet, so Abu Bakr was the best choice as caliph | Ali should have been picked as caliph; the succession should be kept in the family, and Muhammad selected him as a spiritual successor |
| Choosing a leader | Caliphs should be chosen from the Muslim community, by consensus or election | Do not recognise the authority of Sunni Muslim leaders |

The Sunni form the majority of Muslims worldwide.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Caliph** | The successor to Muhammad as leader of the Muslim community, an office both political and religious |
| **Abu Bakr** | Muhammad's father-in-law and close friend, chosen as caliph 632–634 |
| **Ali** | Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, passed over as too young, later named caliph and assassinated in 661 |
| **Sunni** | The 85 per cent who hold that Muhammad cannot be succeeded as prophet, that Abu Bakr was the best choice, and that caliphs should be chosen by the Muslim community |
| **Shi'a** | The 15 per cent who hold that Ali should have been caliph, that succession should stay in Muhammad's family, and who do not recognise Sunni leaders' authority |

# 7.3 The Arab Conquests and the Umayyad Caliphate

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Why embark on conquest?

Four motives are given, and they are worth separating because they are of different kinds.

- Islam united the Arabs under a common cause
- They could become wealthy by taxing conquered peoples
- They had long been oppressed by foreigners
- Conquest was not undertaken for converts; wealth had to be shared

The last point explains an otherwise puzzling feature of the early caliphates: conversion was not the aim, because a conquered population that converted stopped paying the taxes on which the conquerors lived.

## The two empires in the way

### The Sasanian Empire

The Sasanians were the last pre-Islamic heir to the Persian Empire. Power lay in the hands of an autocratic ruler, who was in turn manipulated by wealthy landowners and aristocrats. Muslim victories were rapid; the capital was taken in 651, and with the death of the last ruler Persia was conquered.

### The Byzantine Empire

The Byzantines were defeated at the **Yarmuk River** in 636, and Syria and Egypt were captured by 640. In 642 the Byzantines withdrew from Egypt, which resulted in the spread of Islam across North Africa.

Several factors weakened Byzantine resistance. Some Christians supported the Muslims because of the lower taxes. The empire was overextended and could not resist the Arab advance. Muslim naval supremacy posed a challenge in the Mediterranean, and Muslim invaders and raiders reduced Byzantine strength in North Africa, the Mediterranean and southern Italy.

## Governance and social policy

Non-Muslims in conquered territories were allowed to retain their religion, but paid a tax, the **jizya**, and were exempt from military service.

## The Umayyad Caliphate, 661–750

The Umayyads moved the capital from Medina to **Damascus** and established hereditary rule. The first Umayyad caliph was **Muawiya**. They conquered and united areas through expansion, and governed with a large bureaucracy.

### Social structure

Umayyad society was arranged in a clear hierarchy.

| Group | Position |
|---|---|
| Muslim Arabs | First-class citizens: lower taxes, could join the imperial administration and army, received a share of the riches from conquests |
| Converts to Islam | People could convert, but there was little incentive, since converts were treated as inferior to born Muslims |
| People of the Book | Jews and Christians, treated better than other non-Muslims, paying special taxes called jizya |
| **Dhimmi** | Non-Muslims, who paid taxes |

## The decline of the Umayyads

The causes are internal.

- A decentralised bureaucracy, almost tribal in character, which relied on local rulers
- Religious tensions between Sunnis and Shi'as
- Non-Arab converts to Islam agitating for more rights

The third of these follows directly from the social structure above: a system that gave converts the duties of Muslims without the privileges of Arabs produced exactly the constituency that would bring the dynasty down.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Sasanian Empire** | The last pre-Islamic heir to the Persian Empire, ruled autocratically and conquered by 651 |
| **Yarmuk River** | The 636 battle at which the Arabs defeated the Byzantines, leading to the capture of Syria and Egypt by 640 |
| **Jizya** | The tax paid by non-Muslims, who retained their religion and were exempt from military service |
| **Muawiya** | The first Umayyad caliph |
| **Umayyad Caliphate** | The dynasty of 661–750 that moved the capital to Damascus and established hereditary rule |
| **Dhimmi** | Non-Muslims under Muslim rule, who paid taxes |
| **People of the Book** | Jews and Christians, treated better than other non-Muslims and paying the jizya |

# 7.4 The Abbasid Caliphate and Córdoba

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The Abbasid revolution

The Umayyad caliphs had grown rich and lived luxurious lifestyles, which increased revolts. In 747 the frontier warriors of the Abbasid party made alliances with the Shi'a and with non-Arab Muslim converts — precisely the two groups the Umayyad hierarchy had excluded. In 750 the Abbasids won the **Battle of Zab** and then quickly conquered the rest of the empire.

The Abbasids threw a reconciliation dinner for the Umayyads, which did not end well for the guests. One Umayyad survivor, **Abd al-Rahman I**, fled to the Iberian Peninsula and created the Córdoba Caliphate.

## The Córdoba Caliphate, 756–1031

Córdoba was in **Al-Andalus**, Islamic Spain.

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 711 | The Moors — Berbers, North African Muslims — moved into the Iberian Peninsula |
| 732 | Halted at the Battle of Tours in France |
| 756 | The Umayyads arrived and began the Córdoba Caliphate |

Córdoba preserved Greco-Roman knowledge, and a unique Spanish Arabic style emerged in art, vocabulary and architecture.

## The Abbasid Caliphate, 750–1258

The Abbasids began as Shi'ites but changed to Sunnis, and moved the capital to **Baghdad**, shifting the cultural and political centre eastward.

Their social policy reversed the Umayyad settlement: converts were seen as equal to natural-born Muslims, there were no new taxes, and there was better education and career opportunity. Persian converts came to dominate. The Abbasids did, however, continue the Umayyad style of excess and luxury. **Harems**, households of wives, originate with the Abbasids; within them women could be themselves without men around.

### Growth

Migrations produced massive urbanisation. Building projects included mansions, mosques, baths, schools, resthouses and hospitals; the Abbasids founded totally new cities and modernised old ones.

### Administration and decline

Mercenary armies increased in number: aggressive, and expensive. The Abbasid caliphs became increasingly distracted, and as they did the power of the **wazir**, the chief administrator, increased. The wazir was head of the caliph's inner councils, royal executioner, and the organiser of the administrative infrastructure.

The extravagant living of the upper class, civil wars and increasing taxes produced peasant revolts, religious revolts by the Shi'a, and assassination. Decline began in the mid-ninth century.

**Harun al-Rashid** (786–809) illustrates both sides of the dynasty: a luxurious lifestyle, dependence on Persian advisors, and extravagant building projects, among them the **House of Wisdom** in Baghdad.

## Fragmentation

As Abbasid power weakened, independent states such as the **Fatimids** in Egypt emerged, and the **Seljuk Turks** rose. The **Crusades** (1096–1291) temporarily established Christian rule in parts of the Middle East but had minimal long-term impact.

## Legacy of the Arab Empire

Islam spread widely, shaping the political, cultural and religious landscape across three continents. Internal divisions between Sunni and Shi'ite, together with external pressures from the Crusades and the Mongols, contributed to the eventual fragmentation of the empire.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Battle of Zab** | The 750 victory that gave the Abbasids the empire |
| **Abd al-Rahman I** | The Umayyad survivor who fled to the Iberian Peninsula and created the Córdoba Caliphate |
| **Al-Andalus** | Islamic Spain, seat of the Córdoba Caliphate, 756–1031 |
| **Moors** | Berbers, North African Muslims, who moved into the Iberian Peninsula in 711 |
| **Abbasid Caliphate** | The dynasty of 750–1258 with its capital at Baghdad, which treated converts as equal to born Muslims |
| **Harem** | A household of wives, originating with the Abbasids |
| **Wazir** | The chief administrator, head of the caliph's inner councils and royal executioner, who organised the administrative infrastructure |
| **Harun al-Rashid** | Abbasid caliph (786–809) known for luxury, Persian advisors and extravagant building projects including the House of Wisdom |
| **Fatimids** | An independent state in Egypt that emerged as Abbasid power weakened |
| **Crusades** | 1096–1291; temporarily established Christian rule in parts of the Middle East, with minimal long-term impact |

# 7.5 The Islamic Golden Age

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## A paradox to hold on to

The **Islamic Golden Age** coincides with political decline and social turmoil, not with political strength. Cultural vibrance, an increase in trade and intellectual creativity all rise while the caliphate fragments. By the twelfth century schools, libraries and institutes flourished, with Cairo, Baghdad and Córdoba as the leading centres, drawing on Greek, Roman, Persian and Indian knowledge.

## Trade and urban prosperity

The merchant is honoured in Muslim culture, and the reason is given directly: Muhammad was a merchant.

Between 750 and 1350 a vast trading network was built and the Silk Road was revived, spreading technology, knowledge and culture. The trade networks linked Africa, Asia and Europe, supported by advanced maritime technology and banking systems. **Dhow** ships with **lateen**, or triangular, sails carried the sea trade.

Baghdad was the centre of world trade and education. Muslim workshops produced glassware, jewellery, tapestries, carpets, swords and water clocks. Commercial enterprises and joint ventures were formed with Christians and Jews, and guidelines were formed for artisans to negotiate wages and working conditions.

## Society and social hierarchy

Islamic society was relatively egalitarian for its time, though it practised slavery and maintained gender hierarchies.

## Politics and law

Islam emphasises behaviour and belief together, integrating spiritual and societal duties as guided by the Qur'an and Shari'a law. Early Islamic governance faced challenges in aligning political authority with religious doctrine — the practical difficulty produced by a single framework that is at once religious and political.

## Literature and language

The two languages divided the field between them.

| Language | Domain |
|---|---|
| Persian | The language of high culture |
| Arabic | The language of religion, law and the natural sciences, and the foundation of a great literary tradition |

Calligraphy and illustrated poetry were central art forms. Themes included desert journeys, the joys of battle, chivalry and romance.

## Art and architecture

Islamic art blended geometric patterns, calligraphy and arabesques, avoiding representational images of humans or of the Prophet. Architecture is marked by minarets and mosques; iconic structures include the **Dome of the Rock** and the **Alhambra**.

## Philosophy, science and education

Islamic scholars preserved and expanded upon Greek philosophy and the sciences, making significant contributions in mathematics, astronomy and medicine. Greco-Roman books were copied into Arabic. Education was accompanied by hospitals and by great healthcare.

## Sufism

**Sufism** emerged as a mystical branch of Islam emphasising a personal connection with Allah through music, poetry and dance. It is represented by poets such as **Rumi**.

## Historical writing

Historians such as **al-Mas'udi** and **Ibn Khaldun** advanced historical methods, emphasising critical analysis of sources and the understanding of historical dynamics.

## Integration and legacy

Islamic civilisation absorbed influences from Greek, Persian and Indian traditions while creating enduring contributions in fields such as science, literature and architecture. Its intellectual legacy significantly affected Europe during the medieval and Renaissance periods.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Islamic Golden Age** | The period of cultural vibrance, increased trade and intellectual creativity that accompanied political decline and social turmoil |
| **Dhow** | The ship used in Muslim maritime trade, rigged with lateen sails |
| **Lateen sail** | A triangular sail |
| **Arabesque** | A decorative element of Islamic art, used with geometric patterns and calligraphy in place of representational images |
| **Sufism** | The mystical branch of Islam emphasising personal connection with Allah through music, poetry and dance |
| **Rumi** | The poet who represents Sufism |
| **Al-Mas'udi and Ibn Khaldun** | Historians who advanced historical methods, emphasising critical analysis of sources and historical dynamics |

# 8.1 Africa's Geography, Trade and the Bantu Migrations

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Geographical patterns

Africa's regions are tropical rainforest, savannah and grasslands, and deserts. The land influenced the movement and spread of ideas, people, culture and goods — which is why the geography section comes first: it sets the limits within which every kingdom in this chapter operates.

## The Sahara dries out

The Sahara was once a well-watered area. Ancient rock paintings show rivers and forests. Around 2500 BCE climate change and desertification took place, and people migrated out of the area.

## Resources spur trade

Africa is filled with rich minerals: salt, gold, iron and copper. From 200 CE trading across the Sahara was carried on with caravans, and it brought great profit to the tribes involved.

## The Bantu migrations

West African farmers and herders migrated south and east between 100 BCE and 1000 CE. As Bantu speakers moved, they spread their skills — farming, iron working and domestication. Because they moved into inhabited land rather than empty land, they also mixed their language and culture with the groups they met, and this is why a single language family and a shared set of techniques cover so much of the continent.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Desertification** | The process by which the once well-watered Sahara dried out from around 2500 BCE, causing people to migrate away |
| **Bantu migrations** | The movement of West African farmers and herders south and east between 100 BCE and 1000 CE, spreading farming, iron working and domestication and mixing language and culture |

# 8.2 Nubia, Meroë and Axum

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Nubia rivals Egypt

Trade led to contact between Nubia and Egypt, and the two became rivals for control of the area and of the trade itself.

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 1500 BCE | Nubia comes under Egyptian control for almost 500 years, and adapts many Egyptian traditions |
| 1100 BCE | Nubia gains independence |
| 730 BCE | Nubia takes Egypt |
| 670 BCE | The Assyrians invade Nubia; Nubia retreats south |

## Meroë masters trade

In 500 BCE Nubia moved its capital to **Meroë**, which lay near both the Red Sea and the Nile — a position that put it on two trade systems at once.

## Axum

### Origins

Legend traces the founding of Axum and of the Ethiopian royal dynasty to the son of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, and that dynasty lasted into the twentieth century. The land is first mentioned in a Greek guidebook in 400 CE. Axum's rulers took control of the areas around the Blue Nile and the Red Sea.

### Geography

Axum replaced Kush and was a blend of Africans and Arabs. It was located on the Horn of Africa, in modern Ethiopia.

### Trade

The main cities were **Adulis** and Axum. Axum traded goods and slaves: ivory, spices, stones, hides and gold.

### Culture

Axum blended the cultural traditions of Arab peoples and Kushites. The population of Adulis included Egyptians, Arabians, Greeks, Romans, Persians and Indians, and Greek served as the international lingua franca.

### Religion

Axumite religion was monotheistic, with the king related to God, and included animist beliefs and the honouring of dead animals. International trade brought new ideas, and with them Christianity: by 300 Christianity had come, and King **Ezana** (325–360) made Christianity the official religion. At first Christianity strengthened trade ties. Islam was introduced in the 600s, but Axum did not convert.

### Innovations

- The writing system **Ge'ez**. Axum was the only ancient African kingdom to have a written language besides Egypt and Meroë
- The **Pillars of Axum**, or **stelae**: exploits recorded on stone pillars, built as monuments or tomb markers. They are solid granite, the tallest 100 feet, built without mortar, and carved with false doors, windows and timber beams to celebrate Axumite achievements
- The first sub-Saharan state to mint coins, in bronze, gold and silver
- In agriculture, terrace farming, irrigation canals and dams

### International relations

In 609 Muslim Arabs conquered and occupied cities in North Africa, and in the 700s they conquered the Berbers. Islam replaced Christianity and Arabic replaced Latin and Greek. Islam spread to West Africa and down the East coast.

### The fall of Axum

Axum fell victim to Muslim invasions. In 710 the Muslims destroyed Adulis. Axum retreated into the mountains of northern Ethiopia, isolated, its environment depleted of forests and suffering soil erosion.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Meroë** | The capital to which Nubia moved in 500 BCE, near the Red Sea and the Nile |
| **Axum** | Kingdom on the Horn of Africa, in modern Ethiopia, which replaced Kush and blended Africans and Arabs |
| **Adulis** | Together with Axum, one of the two main cities of the kingdom, with a population of Egyptians, Arabians, Greeks, Romans, Persians and Indians |
| **Ezana** | King of Axum (325–360) who made Christianity the official religion |
| **Ge'ez** | Axum's writing system; Axum was the only ancient African kingdom besides Egypt and Meroë to have a written language |
| **Stelae (Pillars of Axum)** | Solid granite pillars up to 100 feet tall, built without mortar as monuments or tomb markers and carved with false doors, windows and timber beams |

# 8.3 Ethiopia, the East African City-States and Great Zimbabwe

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Ethiopia

Medieval Ethiopia was protected by mountains and unified by Christianity. King **Lalibela** built eleven churches carved underground. Ethiopia kept ties with the Holy Land, and many trade customs, music and dances were incorporated into its sermons.

There is also a Jewish strand. The kings of Ethiopia claimed to be descended from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, a claim reinforced by the fact that they observed Jewish holidays and dietary rules.

## The East African city-states

### Indian Ocean trade

Indian Ocean trade differed from the Silk Roads in one decisive respect: transport costs were much lower, because ships could carry much more at one time than camels could. That single difference changed what was worth carrying. The sea roads carried bulk and staple goods, not just the luxury items of the Silk Road. East Africa exported raw materials — fur, ivory, gold, salt and timber — in return for Indian and Islamic luxuries.

### Monsoons

The **monsoons** are alternating wind currents.

| Season | Direction |
|---|---|
| Summer | Southwest to northeast |
| Winter | Northeast to southwest |

Because the winds reverse, it was easier to sail in particular directions and to trade in different monsoons.

### Trading centres

Trade occurred between individual merchant towns and was not facilitated by major empires. The monsoon winds linked Africa with India. The city-states were generally peaceful. **Kilwa**, **Sofala** and **Mogadishu** were major centres, but the arrangement was more like a set of loose confederacies than a state.

### Swahili

**Swahili** emerged because of these international trading systems, through cultural diffusion and integration. The word is Arabic, meaning "the coast". Swahili buildings were made of coral.

## Great Zimbabwe

Zimbabwe was, in effect, a gold-mining capital and the inland capital of trade. The name is Bantu for "stone houses". It was built by the Bantu people between 900 and 1500, and artefacts show international trade; it was likely a monarchy.

It reached its height around 1300 and began to decline by 1500. The decline is attributed to an inward gold drive, a big population, civil war and dwindling trade.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Lalibela** | King of Ethiopia who built eleven churches carved underground |
| **Monsoons** | Alternating wind currents, blowing southwest to northeast in summer and northeast to southwest in winter, which shaped Indian Ocean sailing and trade |
| **Kilwa, Sofala, Mogadishu** | The major East African trading centres, forming loose confederacies rather than an empire |
| **Swahili** | The coastal culture and language that emerged from international trade; Arabic for "the coast" |
| **Zimbabwe** | Bantu for "stone houses"; an inland gold-mining and trading capital built by the Bantu between 900 and 1500 |

# 9.1 Mesoamerica: Olmec, Zapotec and Maya

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The Olmec civilisation, 1400–300 BCE

The Olmecs were the first civilisation in Mesoamerica and called themselves the **Xi** people. They are known as the **Mother Culture** because their forms spread to the cultures that came after them, and they were the first to use stone in art and architecture. Temples and art indicate powerful priests and nobles. Their most famous artefacts are the **Colossal Heads**, five to eleven feet tall.

### Technological advances

- Magnetic compasses
- Complex drainage and sewer systems
- Complex irrigation and urban piping
- Metallurgy
- Astronomy, to the point that cities were arranged by the stars

### Influence

The Olmecs traded with their neighbours, and cultural diffusion carried jaguars, serpents, calendars and hieroglyphics outward.

### Society and religion

The chief held the highest rank, and there were few "status" positions. Labour was collective. The ball game was played. Religion and society were one and the same.

Olmec religion was polytheistic and animistic, with ten deities with dual characteristics. It involved blood letting and human sacrifice. Jaguars stood for rulers, alongside snakes, crocodiles and sharks; shamans and healers assumed animal powers.

### Decline

There are few decipherable written records, and nobody really knows how the Olmecs declined.

## The Zapotecs, 500 BCE–1000 CE

The Zapotecs had traditions similar to the Olmecs: a small ruling class, aggressive conquerors, human sacrifice, hieroglyphics that recorded conquests, and ball games.

They were the first great stone pyramid builders. Their centre was **Monte Albán**, and their major cities were Monte Albán and San José Mogote. Efficient agriculture plus an advanced irrigation system produced a population boom. Like the Olmecs they had calendars, pyramids, temples, palaces, an observatory and stone sculptures.

## The Maya

The Maya were influenced by the Olmecs.

### Farming

Maya farming used **slash and burn** and raised fields along riverbanks. The guide is blunt that this was not, in fact, effective and drained nutrition from the soil. Even so, at their height the Maya achieved a massive surplus and a population boom, storing grain in **chultunes**, underground granaries.

### Politics

The Maya had powerful city-states. They were never an empire and were not politically united, but they traded regularly: honey, salt, cotton and cacao, and feathers, jade and jaguar pelts.

### Religion

Sacrifice used people captured in battle. The Maya worshipped hundreds of gods, with overlap in their duties, and made human sacrifices for important events. Kings and priests propitiated the gods.

### Astronomy

The Maya kept two calendars: a ritual calendar of 260 days and a solar calendar of 365 days.

### Decline

Cities were abandoned around 900 CE, and by 1500 Maya settlement was mostly villages. Nobody knows what caused the decline.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Xi** | The Olmecs' name for themselves |
| **Mother Culture** | The Olmecs, so called because their culture spread to those that came after them |
| **Colossal Heads** | Olmec stone heads, five to eleven feet tall |
| **Monte Albán** | The Zapotec centre and, with San José Mogote, one of their major cities |
| **Slash and burn** | Maya farming method, used with raised fields along riverbanks; not effective and nutrition-draining |
| **Chultunes** | Maya underground granaries |

markdown:
# 9.2 Teotihuacan, the Toltecs and the Aztecs

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Teotihuacan, 100–650 CE

Teotihuacan is a city of pyramids. The Aztecs later called it "place of the gods". Its writing and language did not survive, so the city is known through its goods and its plan: obsidian, rubber, cacao, feathers, food and **pulque**, a liquor.

As a city of gods it was the largest in the region, with around 200,000 people, and contained temples, markets, workshops and residences. It borrowed the ball game and the calendar from the Olmecs. It was planned religiously and astronomically, and fed by floating gardens and irrigation.

## The Toltecs

Various groups in relative isolation formed an empire, with its capital at **Tula** in 968. Toltec influence reached beyond central Mexico, and they traded with the American Southwest. **Quetzalcoatl** belongs to their tradition.

Toltec society was militaristic, a conquest state ruled by two chieftains. It was agrarian and traded feathers, jade, gold and obsidian. It practised human sacrifice. Its decline in 1122 is unexplained.

## The Aztecs

The Valley of Mexico is the high plateau of central Mexico.

### The Mexica

The **Mexica** were the group who migrated from the north in the early thirteenth century and spoke **Nahuatl**.

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 1325 | Founded Tenochtitlan |
| 1434 | Conquered the surrounding city-states |

The founding of Tenochtitlan is told in Aztec legend; the site was Lake Texcoco, a swampy lake.

### The Triple Alliance

The **Triple Alliance** joined the Mexica of Tenochtitlan with Texcoco and Tlacopan, and covered a population of five to six million. Tribute from subject peoples was what allowed the Aztecs to build up Tenochtitlan.

### Flower Wars

The **Flower Wars** were intermittent ritual wars between the Triple Alliance and subject city-states and rival neighbours, fought over many years. Combatants met at predetermined sites with equal numbers of forces, and fought small-scale battles with melee weapons to show individual skill. They were generally less deadly than real wars.

### Tenochtitlan

Tenochtitlan was influenced by the city of Teotihuacan and was well planned. It had the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon, and was the site where the gods made the Aztec world.

### Government and society

A single ruler was elected by a council of nobles, priests and military leaders, below whom came the noble administration, warriors and priests.

### Economy

The Aztec economy was agrarian. Man-made floating islands yielded large amounts of crops, organised by clans, growing maize and beans. Vibrant daily markets were regulated by the state.

### Religion

Aztec religion was polytheistic.

| Deity | Role |
|---|---|
| **Huitzilopochtli** | Patron god of the Aztecs, deity of war and the sun, patron of Tenochtitlan |
| **Nanahuatzin** | Sacrificed himself to become the sun; sacrifices were made to give strength to the sun, usually of prisoners of war |
| **Quetzalcoatl** | The feathered serpent god, of learning and culture |

### Knowledge

The Aztecs kept historical records in hieroglyphics, used a calendar inspired by the Maya, and practised a medicine that was almost entirely herbal.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Pulque** | A liquor traded at Teotihuacan |
| **Tula** | The Toltec capital, founded 968 |
| **Mexica** | The group who migrated from the north in the early thirteenth century, spoke Nahuatl and founded Tenochtitlan in 1325 |
| **Nahuatl** | The language of the Mexica |
| **Triple Alliance** | The alliance of the Mexica of Tenochtitlan with Texcoco and Tlacopan |
| **Flower Wars** | Intermittent ritual wars fought at predetermined sites with equal forces and melee weapons, less deadly than real wars |
| **Huitzilopochtli** | Patron god of the Aztecs, deity of war and the sun and patron of Tenochtitlan |
| **Nanahuatzin** | The deity who sacrificed himself to become the sun |
| **Quetzalcoatl** | The feathered serpent god, of learning and culture |

# 9.3 North and South America

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## North America

### The Eastern Woodlands

Agriculture began in the third millennium BCE, focusing on maize, squash, beans and grasses. Sedentary villages emerged, with councils to resolve disputes, and some regions united under chiefs. Trade networks spanned from Lake Superior to the Gulf of Mexico, exchanging goods such as meat, shells and tools.

### Cahokia

**Cahokia** was a major urban centre near modern-day East St Louis, Illinois, with large earthen mounds. It served as an administrative and trade hub, and there is evidence of Mesoamerican influences, such as ball courts. It declined by the twelfth century, possibly for environmental or social reasons.

### The Ancient Pueblo peoples

The Ancient Pueblo peoples developed agriculture in the arid Southwest — Colorado, New Mexico and Arizona — and built adobe pueblos such as Chaco Canyon, with advanced irrigation systems and trade networks. Possible reasons for their migration in the thirteenth century include drought, warfare, or external pressures, with evidence of cannibalism. Their descendants include the Hopi and Zuni tribes. Note the relation carefully: all Hopi are Pueblo, but not all Pueblo are Hopi.

## South America

### Caral, Peru

**Caral** was one of the earliest urban centres, dating from 2500 BCE, with pyramids, plazas and astronomical structures; it is arguably an early civilisation next to Mesopotamia. It practised irrigation farming and traded with coastal communities in cotton, fish and reeds. There is evidence of social stratification and of cultural activities such as music and crafts.

### Chavín

The **Chavín** culture emerged in the first millennium BCE and is known for stone temples and metallurgy in copper and gold. It declined by 200 BCE, leaving behind artistic and religious influences.

### Moche

The **Moche** of Peru, in the first millennium CE, were an advanced civilisation with adobe pyramids such as the Pyramid of the Sun, and intricate art in ceramics and metalwork. They focused on warfare, sacrifice and astronomy, including **Ai Apaec**, the Decapitator God. They collapsed by the eighth century because of environmental disruptions such as El Niño floods and drought. Little is known about their culture, which survives through artefacts.

### Wari and Chimú

The **Wari** expanded into Moche territories as the Moche declined. The **Chimú** built **Chan Chan**, a large adobe city with advanced irrigation systems. Chimú civilisation collapsed by the fifteenth century when floods and earthquakes damaged their irrigation systems.

## Environmental impact on civilisations

This section pulls the chapter together, and it is worth treating as an argument rather than a list. Climate changes — droughts and floods — contributed to the fall of the Moche, of the Mayan city-states, and possibly of the Roman Empire. Overuse of land in Mesopotamia and in the Maya regions led to soil erosion and decline.

**El Niño** caused alternating droughts and floods, damaging agriculture and fishing industries. It is followed by **La Niña**, which brings hurricanes. Notice that the Moche and the Chimú were both destroyed by water damage to the systems that made their farming possible: in an irrigation civilisation, the weather is a political event.

## Cultural and religious practices

Moche rituals included human sacrifices to invoke rain or prevent disasters. The Wari adopted and repurposed Moche religious symbols and buildings. Precious artefacts were often placed in burial sites, reflecting cultural values.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Cahokia** | Major urban centre near modern East St Louis, Illinois, with large earthen mounds; an administrative and trade hub showing Mesoamerican influence; declined by the twelfth century |
| **Ancient Pueblo peoples** | Farmers of the arid Southwest who built adobe pueblos such as Chaco Canyon; ancestors of the Hopi and Zuni |
| **Caral** | One of the earliest urban centres (2500 BCE, Peru), with pyramids, plazas and astronomical structures |
| **Chavín** | First-millennium-BCE culture known for stone temples and metallurgy in copper and gold |
| **Moche** | First-millennium-CE Peruvian civilisation with adobe pyramids and intricate ceramics and metalwork, collapsed by the eighth century through environmental disruption |
| **Ai Apaec** | The Moche Decapitator God |
| **Chan Chan** | The large adobe city with advanced irrigation built by the Chimú |
| **El Niño** | The pattern causing alternating droughts and floods, damaging agriculture and fishing; followed by La Niña, which brings hurricanes |
