# 10.1 China After the Han: The Sui and the Tang

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Division and civil war

After the collapse of the Han came a period of division and civil war. In the absence of organised government, nomadic forces from the Gobi desert took over northern China.

In the south, Chinese rule was maintained, in what is called the **Era of Six Dynasties**. Its intellectual character is a reaction: Confucian principles of hard work, community interests and rational order were rejected, and people sought emotional satisfaction instead, through hedonistic pursuits and philosophical Daoism. The **Seven Sages of the Bamboo Forest** were a group of writers of this kind, among them the poet Liu Liang.

Daoism, however, could not satisfy deeper emotional needs, and Buddhism filled the gap in the first and second centuries. The sequence matters: each ideology enters because the previous one has failed at something.

## The Sui dynasty

After four years of internal division China was unified in 581, when **Yang Jian**, known as **Sui Wendi**, founded the Sui. The capital was Chang'an.

The Sui created a unified ideology to enhance efficiency, combining Confucianism with Daoism and Buddhism. Monasteries for both doctrines were founded in the capital and Buddhist monks were appointed to key positions as political advisers.

The great Sui project was the construction of the **Grand Canal**, which linked the Yellow and Yangzi rivers. Its effects were three:

- It facilitated the shipment of grain and commodities from the rice-rich southern provinces to the north
- It speeded communication
- It permitted the rapid dispatch of troops to troubled provinces

### Fall

The Sui ended at the death of **Sui Yangdi**, Wendi's son, after a short reign. **Li Yuan**, one of Sui Yangdi's generals, took advantage of the instability and founded the Tang dynasty.

## The Tang dynasty

Li Yuan's reign was short, and his son **Tang Taizong** took over. The Tang programme was internal renewal and external expansion.

- The northwest was pacified and given the name **Xinjiang**
- A long conflict with Tibet extended Chinese control over the plateau north of the Himalayas
- The southern provinces were assimilated into the Chinese Empire, and the imperial court established commercial and diplomatic relations with the states of Southeast Asia

China was now the foremost power in East Asia, and the emperor demanded tribute from beyond the frontier. Korea accepted tributary status and attempted to adapt the Chinese model; the Japanese dispatched official missions to China to learn.

### The flowering of culture

The Tang saw the apogee of Chinese creativity and sculpture. The cause given is Buddhism, which affected art, literature, philosophy, religion and politics. Monasteries multiplied, Buddhist monks served as advisors at court, and Chang'an became the seat of empire.

### Fall

Internal forces rose: court intrigues and official corruption, and droughts. In 755 rebellious forces seized control of Chang'an. The forces were suppressed, but the situation of the Tang never fully recovered.

The loss of government power had two consequences that fed each other: the great landed families increased in strength, and there was chronic instability along the northern and western frontiers, where local military commanders ruled without the government.

The end came when the **Kirghiz**, a nomadic people, defeated the Uighurs and overthrew the Tang government, leaving chaos — foreign invasion and division.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Era of Six Dynasties** | The southern period after the Han in which Confucian principles were rejected in favour of emotional satisfaction, hedonistic pursuits and philosophical Daoism |
| **Seven Sages of the Bamboo Forest** | A group of writers of the Era of Six Dynasties, including the poet Liu Liang |
| **Yang Jian (Sui Wendi)** | Founder of the Sui dynasty, who unified China in 581 with his capital at Chang'an |
| **Grand Canal** | The Sui construction linking the Yellow and Yangzi rivers, which moved grain north, speeded communication and allowed rapid troop movement |
| **Li Yuan** | A general of Sui Yangdi who founded the Tang dynasty |
| **Tang Taizong** | Li Yuan's son, under whom the Tang pursued internal renewal and external expansion |
| **Xinjiang** | The name given to the pacified northwest |
| **Kirghiz** | The nomadic people who defeated the Uighurs and overthrew the Tang government |

# 10.2 The Song Dynasty and the Confucian State

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The Song, 960–1279

At the start the Song rulers had problems defending their territory. **Song Taizu**, the founding emperor, was unable to reconquer all of the northwest of the country from the Khitan people. The capital was **Kaifeng**, but under pressure from nomads in the north the capital moved to **Hangzhou**; the seven emperors who ruled from Hangzhou are known as the **Southern Song**.

The Song were a period of economic expansion, prosperity and cultural achievement, but of political and military weakness, and it was the second that decided their fate: they were not able to surmount external challenges from the north.

## The fall of the Song

In their final decades the Song rulers had to pay tribute to the **Jurchen** people of Manchuria. In the thirteenth century they formed an alliance with the Mongols. After defeating the Jurchens, the Mongols turned on the Song. The Song, weakened by internal factionalism and the loss of tax revenues, were defeated — with gunpowder — and the **Yuan dynasty** was created.

## Confucianism and the machinery of government

Chinese government in this period was based on principles originally established during the Qin and Han, and this Confucian order emerged from the Sui to the end of the Song.

| Level | Body and function |
|---|---|
| Apex | The **Grand Council**, assisted by a secretariat and chancellery, with representatives from three authorities: military, civil and censorate |
| Below | The **Department of Affairs**, composed of ministries responsible for justice, military affairs, personnel, public works, revenue and rites |

The effectiveness of the Department of Affairs was limited, for two reasons: it administered only in the capital city, and its processes were dominated by aristocrats.

## The examination system

The Song response to aristocratic dominance was the examination. The Song limited aristocratic control over the bureaucracy and strengthened the power of the central administration by making the examination the primary route to an official career.

| Period | Examination content |
|---|---|
| Early Tang | Questions on Buddhist, Daoist and Confucian texts |
| Song | Based on Confucianism |

The Song tried to open up the system to provide equal opportunity for the poor and the affluent, and set up training academies at provincial and district levels. The class produced by this system is the **scholar-gentry**.

## Local government

The Song maintained the local government institutions of their predecessors. The **magistrate** was responsible for law and order. Village government was by a council of elders, assisted by a chief, who maintained the militia and collected and delivered taxes.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Song Taizu** | The founding Song emperor, unable to reconquer the northwest from the Khitan people |
| **Southern Song** | The seven emperors who ruled from Hangzhou after the capital moved from Kaifeng under pressure from northern nomads |
| **Jurchen** | The people of Manchuria to whom the Song had to pay tribute in their final decades |
| **Grand Council** | The apex of the government hierarchy, assisted by secretariat and chancellery, with representatives from the military, civil and censorate authorities |
| **Department of Affairs** | The body of ministries for justice, military affairs, personnel, public works, revenue and rites, limited to the capital and dominated by aristocrats |
| **Scholar-gentry** | The class produced by making the Confucian examination the primary route to an official career |
| **Magistrate** | The local official responsible for law and order |

# 10.3 Economy, Manufacturing and the Silk Road

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The Chinese economy in this period rests on three legs: agriculture, commerce and manufacturing.

## Land under the Tang

At the rise of the Tang, land was in the hands of noble families and peasants were in slavery. Under **Empress Wu** the government moved to reduce the power of the landed nobility and to maximise tax revenues by adopting the ancient **well-field system**, in which land was allocated to farmers for life in return for an annual tax payment and three weeks of conscript labour.

The reform did not hold. The rich and the politically influential manipulated the system for their own benefit and accumulated huge tracts of land. With population growth and a rise in food production, the government abandoned the effort to equalise landholdings and returned the land to private hands — a retreat that contributed to the fall of the dynasty.

## Land under the Song

The Song returned to reducing the power of the wealthy landed aristocrats. **Wang Anshi** (1021–1086) attempted to limit the size of landholdings through progressive land taxes, and provided cheap credit to poor farmers to help them avoid bankruptcy.

Agricultural prosperity also came from three practical changes:

- The opening of new lands in the Yangzi River valley
- Improvements in irrigation techniques, such as the **chain pump**
- The introduction of a new strain of quick-growing rice from Southeast Asia

## Manufacturing

| Product | Development |
|---|---|
| Steel | Mastered by mixing cast iron and wrought iron, producing swords, armour and sickles |
| Textiles | Cotton from India supported textile production |
| Gunpowder | Developed under the Tang dynasty |

## The Silk Road

Chinese military forts were established at strategic points along the edge of the Taklimakan Desert and out to the borders of Central Asia. The trade itself was carried by **Uighurs**, who were Turkic-speaking, and **Sogdians**, who were Iranian-speaking, with Bactrian camel caravans transporting goods across regions.

Route choice was governed by risk. The southern Taklimakan route had bandits; the direct Uighur hinterland route was avoided; and the mountain routes were arduous because of dryness.

Chang'an was wealthy in the Tang era, but it faced drought and supply issues as well as threats from Turkic-speaking groups and from rebels. **Dunhuang** served as a secondary Tang capital.

The marine route became appealing after the fall of the Tang dynasty in the tenth century — the overland system depended on garrisons and a strong dynasty, and when those went, trade moved to the sea.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Well-field system** | The ancient system revived under Empress Wu, allocating land to farmers for life in return for an annual tax payment and three weeks of conscript labour |
| **Wang Anshi** | Song reformer (1021–1086) who tried to limit landholdings through progressive land taxes and gave cheap credit to poor farmers |
| **Chain pump** | An improved irrigation technique of the Song period |
| **Uighurs** | Turkic-speaking traders of the Silk Road |
| **Sogdians** | Iranian-speaking traders of the Silk Road |
| **Dunhuang** | A secondary Tang capital on the Silk Road |

markdown:
# 10.4 In Search of the Way

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The arrival and early spread of Buddhism and Daoism

Buddhism came to China with Indian travellers. During the decline of the Han dynasty, Buddhism and Daoism offered spiritual solace to those seeking more than Confucianism could give — Confucianism was a doctrine of order and duty, and it had little to say to people whose order had collapsed. The Silk Road facilitated the spread of Buddhism.

## Buddhism becomes Chinese

Buddhism took on Chinese characteristics and split into sects.

| Sect | Emphasis |
|---|---|
| **Chan** (Zen) | Meditation |
| **Pure Land** | Devotion |
| **White Lotus** | Political aspirations |

Buddhism gradually integrated into daily life.

## The decline of Buddhism and Daoism

In the later Tang, Buddhism and Daoism lost court favour. Two reasons are given: envy from other groups, and their own accumulation of wealth and land. Success at court was what made them vulnerable at court.

## The rise of Neo-Confucianism

**Neo-Confucianism** emerged to fill the ideological void left by the decline of Buddhism and Daoism, and aimed to strengthen the state's power.

**Zhu Xi** combined the Confucian classics with Buddhist and Daoist metaphysics and emphasised the investigation of things. His ideas were central to Confucian ideology, but faced criticism from scholars such as **Wang Yangming**.

Neo-Confucianism emphasised the search of the inner self and incorporated Buddhist concepts such as karma, which in turn influenced Confucian views on hierarchy. The movement therefore does not simply replace Buddhism; it absorbs it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Chan (Zen)** | The Buddhist sect emphasising meditation |
| **Pure Land** | The Buddhist sect focusing on devotion |
| **White Lotus** | The Buddhist sect with political aspirations |
| **Neo-Confucianism** | The movement that emerged to fill the ideological void left by the decline of Buddhism and Daoism, aiming to strengthen the state's power, emphasising the inner self and incorporating Buddhist concepts such as karma |
| **Zhu Xi** | The thinker who combined the Confucian classics with Buddhist and Daoist metaphysics and emphasised the investigation of things |
| **Wang Yangming** | A scholar who criticised Zhu Xi's ideas |

# 10.5 Changing Social Conditions in Traditional China

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## A more complex society

From the end of the Han to the Ming dynasty, Chinese society became more complex. Urban populations grew, and the social structure diversified with more merchants, artisans and other groups.

## The rise of the gentry

In the early Tang, powerful noble families held sway. The civil service examination system led to the rise of the **scholar-gentry**, who replaced the aristocracy in influence. This is the social consequence of an administrative reform: once office depended on examination rather than birth, the men who passed examinations became the leading class.

## Village and family life

Under the Ming, most Chinese lived in villages.

## The role of women

Despite male-dominant traditions there were changes. In the Tang, some women were politically active. In the Song, **foot-binding** became common among the gentry. Women also had economic roles, for example in silk production and in running businesses.

## Technological advances

Paper was invented in China. Woodblock printing emerged by the first century BCE, and by the seventh century Chinese craftsmen had advanced wood-carving and printing techniques.

## Literature

### Poetry

**Li Bo** and **Du Fu** were the prominent Tang poets, and the contrast between them is the point.

| Poet | Character of the work |
|---|---|
| Li Bo | A carefree, imaginative style |
| Du Fu | Poems reflecting the social and political turmoil of the late Tang |

### Prose and history

After the Han era, historical writing and essays remained popular literary forms, and each dynasty produced an official history of its predecessor. The great novels are *The Romance of the Three Kingdoms* and *The Water Margin*.

### Entertainment

With the growth of cities, popular entertainment thrived: comedians, musicians, boxers, acrobats, marionettes, shadow plays and storytellers.

## Art

Painting in China reached a high level of excellence under the Tang dynasty. Influenced by Buddhism and Daoism, which emphasised nature, Chinese painters developed **mountain-water painting**.

**Porcelain**, made of fine clay baked at high temperatures, was first produced after the fall of the Han and became popular during the Tang.

In sculpture, the increase in Silk Road trade during the Tang is directly visible: ceramic sculptures of horses and camels were created as tomb figures.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Scholar-gentry** | The class raised by the civil service examination system, which replaced the aristocracy in influence |
| **Foot-binding** | A practice that became common among the gentry in the Song |
| **Li Bo** | Tang poet of carefree, imaginative style |
| **Du Fu** | Tang poet whose work reflected the social and political turmoil of the late Tang |
| **Mountain-water painting** | The Chinese painting form developed under the influence of Buddhism and Daoism, which emphasised nature |
| **Porcelain** | Ceramic of fine clay baked at high temperatures, first produced after the fall of the Han and popular during the Tang |

# 10.6 The Ming Dynasty

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The Ming ruled from 1368 to 1644, having replaced the Yuan.

## Political and administrative reforms

Emperor **Hongwu** established family representatives for provincial governance and expanded printing, which spread Confucian materials. He restored the civil service examination, accessible to all classes and based on Confucian texts, and reinstated traditional Confucian institutions, using the examinations to select bureaucrats and dividing the empire for administration.

He also implemented agricultural initiatives and policies to ensure fairness in management, including land redistribution and irrigation projects.

**The Ming Code** was a unified legal code, intended to promote clarity and sustainability, with defined punishments.

## Economic and infrastructure developments

- Restoration of the **Grand Canal**, which improved trade and employment
- Strengthening of the **Great Wall**. The Ming built part of the Great Wall for protection against northern invasions, and used it to fortify the northern frontier
- The **Imyiwei**, the embroidered uniform guard, founded by Hongwu, which evolved into a military organisation and a spy network

## Expansion and foreign relations

The Ming expanded their rule into Mongolia and Central Asia and briefly reconquered Vietnam. They maintained a tributary relationship with Korea.

## The Yongle emperor

**Yongle** rebelled against the Jianwen emperor, his nephew. His reign is marked by:

- Moving the capital to Beijing, with the Forbidden City and palace
- A eunuch secret police
- An expanded civil service system
- The **Yongle Encyclopedia**

### The economy under Yongle

The goals were the revitalisation of cities and the reconstruction of the Grand Canal, with an emphasis on agriculture alongside textile and porcelain manufacturing. Communities became less isolated as the distance between market towns decreased, and the Ming boasted the largest economy.

## Zheng He's voyages

In 1405 the Yongle emperor sent **Zheng He** on voyages with a large fleet that reached the east coast of Africa. Three reasons are given for them: trade expansion, alliance building and power projection. The voyages continued after his death.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Hongwu** | The first Ming emperor, who established family representatives for provincial governance, expanded printing, restored the civil service exam and pursued land redistribution and irrigation |
| **The Ming Code** | A unified legal code promoting clarity and sustainability, with defined punishments |
| **Imyiwei** | The embroidered uniform guard founded by Hongwu, which evolved into a military organisation and spy network |
| **Yongle** | The emperor who rebelled against his nephew the Jianwen emperor, moved the capital to Beijing and built the Forbidden City |
| **Yongle Encyclopedia** | The great compilation produced under the Yongle emperor |
| **Zheng He** | The admiral sent by Yongle in 1405 with a large fleet that reached the east coast of Africa |

# 11.1 Korea

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Early settlement and a historical dispute

The Korean peninsula was likely first settled by Altaic-speaking fishing and hunting people from Manchuria during the Neolithic Age.

Which kingdom came first is disputed, and the dispute runs along national lines.

| Source | Claim |
|---|---|
| Chinese sources | Koguryo (37 BCE–668 CE) was the first organised kingdom |
| Korean scholars | **Gojoseon**, founded by **Dangun** in 2333 BCE, was the first, with an ethnically Korean population |

## Chinese influence and the Three Kingdoms, fourth to seventh centuries

In 109 BCE the northern part of the Korean peninsula came under direct Chinese rule during the Han dynasty.

The **Three Kingdoms** were **Koguryo**, **Paekche** and **Silla**. Koguryo was the first to introduce Buddhism, in the late fourth century CE, and established Confucian academies. Silla was initially less influenced by China but later became dominant. Silla accepted tributary status under the Tang dynasty in order to appease the Chinese and unify the country — a submission used as a tool of unification.

## The Koryo dynasty, ninth to fourteenth centuries

Silla collapsed in the early tenth century, and the **Koryo** dynasty emerged in the north. It aimed to strengthen its power by introducing Chinese political institutions, and lasted about four hundred years, a period of high achievement.

Buddhist monasteries were significant in Koryo: they controlled large territories, provided Buddhist monks as royal advisers, and produced art, including the printing of the **Tripitaka** on wooden blocks.

### Decline

In the thirteenth century the Mongols seized the northern part of Korea and made it a tributary of the Yuan empire. The Koryo kingdom also struggled to overcome the power of the nobility. During the Mongol invasion, Korean peasants and artisans were compelled to provide conscript labour for shipbuilding for Kublai Khan's invasion of Japan.

## Choson

The **Choson** kingdom actively adopted new technologies from China, such as woodblock printing.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Gojoseon** | The kingdom founded by Dangun in 2333 BCE, held by Korean scholars to be the first, with an ethnically Korean population |
| **Three Kingdoms** | Koguryo, Paekche and Silla |
| **Koguryo** | The kingdom of 37 BCE–668 CE, first to introduce Buddhism in the late fourth century CE and to establish Confucian academies |
| **Silla** | Initially less influenced by China, later dominant; accepted tributary status under the Tang to appease China and unify the country |
| **Koryo** | The dynasty that emerged after Silla's collapse, lasting about four hundred years and introducing Chinese political institutions |
| **Tripitaka** | The Buddhist scripture printed on wooden blocks under the Koryo |
| **Choson** | The kingdom that actively adopted new technologies from China, such as woodblock printing |

# 11.2 Classical Japan

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Geography

Japan is an archipelago of 14,125 islands, of which Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu are the main ones. Between 70 and 80 per cent of the land is mountainous, with rain and short rivers. Japan sits on the ring of fire, and has volcanoes, earthquakes and tsunamis. It also has many natural harbours and ports. The result is a distinct "island culture".

## Early Japan

The earliest inhabitants were the **Jomon** people, some 10,000 years ago, who lived by hunting, fishing and food-gathering. By 800 BCE rice cultivation had been introduced, possibly by Korean immigrants.

The **Yayoi** (300 BCE–250 CE) were a mixture of the Jomon people and the newly arriving Koreans. They lived at first on Kyushu, then settled on the Yamato plain in the vicinity of the modern cities of Osaka and Kyoto. Society was highly decentralised. In the year 57 Japan was first mentioned in Chinese records, as scattered farming tribal communities.

## The Yamato period, 250–710

The Yamato period divides into two.

### Kofun, 250–538

Shintoism and burial mounds, with decentralised chieftains.

### Asuka, 538–710

Japan dealt with China in two ways: by an alliance with Korea, and by having a centralised authority.

**Shotoku Taishi** (572–622) sent missions to the Tang to learn, and instituted the **Taika Reforms**. Buddhism arrived. The **Fujiwara** then took power, and kept the Taika Reforms: a centralised bureaucracy, lowered taxes, officialised Buddhism and written scripts. Civil service examinations were adopted but limited to the aristocracy, which is where Japan differs from China — the examination in China opened the bureaucracy to new men, whereas in Japan it confirmed the men already there.

The ruler was styled "Son of Heaven", and the capital moved to Nara, modelled after Chang'an.

## The Nara period, 710–794

Nara's success was due mostly to the power of landowning elites, and Buddhist monasteries were gaining land.

## Early Japanese culture

Chinese influence runs through it. Japan took the three core philosophies and added **Shintoism**, which involved landscapes, history and ancestral ties.

| Field | Feature |
|---|---|
| Writing | Kanji, Katakana and Hiragana — two different versions of written Japanese |
| Arts | Poetry, painting and architecture all heavily influenced by the Tang |
| Clothing | The kimono, and samurai uniforms |
| Entertainment | Wrestling, martial arts, music and games such as go |
| Technology | Paper-making |
| Daily life | A sitting posture close to the floor |

## The Heian period

Heian is the "Golden Age" of Japanese culture. Men wrote in Chinese and women wrote in Japanese, and the court was segregated along the same line.

Heian is also the end of the classical period, because of what happened to power. The emperor became a figurehead and the Chancellor, the **Kwampaku**, ruled in the emperor's name while "protecting" the emperor in seclusion. The chancellorship gathered more and more power, which spread to the military, and imperial power dissolved.

### Decline

Disunity followed. The Fujiwara clan neglected the military and delegated responsibility to warrior clans, which decentralised power and produced many clan quarrels. The **Taira–Minamoto War** (1156–1185) destroyed the Fujiwara clan by 1160, and the Minamoto won.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Jomon** | The earliest inhabitants of Japan, hunters, fishers and food-gatherers of some 10,000 years ago |
| **Yayoi** | The people of 300 BCE–250 CE, a mixture of Jomon and arriving Koreans, who settled the Yamato plain |
| **Kofun** | The Yamato sub-period of 250–538, of Shintoism, burial mounds and decentralised chieftains |
| **Asuka** | The Yamato sub-period of 538–710, of alliance with Korea and centralised authority |
| **Shotoku Taishi** | Ruler (572–622) who sent missions to the Tang and instituted the Taika Reforms |
| **Taika Reforms** | The reforms kept by the Fujiwara: centralised bureaucracy, lowered taxes, officialised Buddhism and written scripts |
| **Shintoism** | The Japanese religion involving landscapes, history and ancestral ties |
| **Kwampaku** | The Chancellor who ruled in the emperor's name while keeping the emperor in seclusion |
| **Taira–Minamoto War** | The war of 1156–1185 which destroyed the Fujiwara clan by 1160 and was won by the Minamoto |

markdown:
# 11.3 Medieval and Early Modern Japan

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The Minamoto and the Kamakura shogunate

The Minamoto created the **Shogunate**, which the guide calls Japan's "Fall of Rome" moment: the transition from classical to medieval. The capital was at Kamakura, founded by **Minamoto Yoritomo**, and the government was a decentralised military one. The emperor was now only a figurehead; the **shoguns** held the real power. The **Bakufu**, the military administration, was established.

There was a struggle for power after Yoritomo's death in 1199, and in the **Jokyu Disturbance** of 1221 Kamakura defeated Kyoto.

## The power structure

The shogun delegated power to local lords, who eventually became the **daimyo** and who came from the warrior clans. **Samurai** means "the ones who serve".

One detail is worth marking, because it distinguishes Japan from a straightforward system of land tenure: lords were not granted land for service, but titles, which could be revoked. Japan eventually broke from China.

Samurai were soldiers with a master; **ronin** were soldiers without masters, and ranked lower than samurai.

## Religion and law

Zen Buddhism arrives in 1191, and the Lotus Sutra sect, described as radical and intolerant, in 1253.

In 1232 the **Joei Shikimoku** legal code reflected Confucian values. Before it, disputes had been settled through social connections.

## The decline of Kamakura

Kamakura lost power to landlords. The **Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281** were defeated by quick military mobilisation, but they brought financial strain and a loss of loyalty. In 1331 the revolt of Emperor **Go-Daigo** restored imperial power briefly, producing a short period with two governments.

## The samurai, more closely

The guide corrects several assumptions.

- Samurai were not just full-time warriors: they were also scholars, bureaucrats, and practitioners of the arts — music, literature and poetry
- They were not always "good and faithful": they could turn on their clan for a better offer of stipend
- They were not only men
- **Bushido** — justice, courage, mercy, politeness, honesty, honour, loyalty and self-control — has no record before the mid-nineteenth century and the Second World War

## The Muromachi or Ashikaga period

The founder was **Ashikaga Takauji**. For the first fifty-odd years there were two imperial courts: Go-Daigo established the southern court in 1336, and Takauji appointed himself shogun in Kyoto with the northern court in 1338. The southern court surrendered and Japan was unified again in 1392.

Culture flowered. **Noh drama** combined masks, art and poetry with increased Zen influence. **Ashikaga Yoshimitsu** (1368–1408) maintained good trade relations with Ming China. Domestic prosperity — improved agriculture and the development of markets — produced growing urbanisation and new social classes.

The Ashikaga gradually lost influence over the outer regions, which is what allowed the rise of the powerful daimyo.

## The Warring States

The **Sengoku period**, 1467–1568, was a century-long civil war between six main families and many smaller rivals. In 1542 the Portuguese brought guns and Christianity.

## The Tokugawa

Three great unifiers end the wars.

| Unifier | Achievement |
|---|---|
| Oda Nobunaga | Destroyed the Ashikaga by 1573 |
| Toyotomi Hideyoshi | By 1590 brought most of Japan under his rule |
| Tokugawa Ieyasu | In 1600 defeated Ishida Mitsunari at the Battle of Sekigahara, finishing the unification of Japan |

Tokugawa was named shogun in 1603, and the Tokugawa ruled Japan until 1868. They were determined to end feudal warfare, and introduced new laws to control society and uphold a new moral code.

The result was an economic boom, with internal trade flourishing, and the development of the arts. **Kabuki** developed in the 1600s: less refined, with less Buddhist influence, and including comedy. Japanese painting developed its own styles — landscapes, historical events and simple lines.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Shogunate** | The military government created by the Minamoto, marking the transition from classical to medieval Japan |
| **Bakufu** | The military administration established under the shogunate |
| **Jokyu Disturbance** | The 1221 conflict in which Kamakura defeated Kyoto |
| **Daimyo** | The local lords to whom the shogun delegated power, drawn from the warrior clans |
| **Samurai** | "The ones who serve"; soldiers with a master, who were also scholars, bureaucrats and artists |
| **Ronin** | Soldiers without masters, ranked lower than samurai |
| **Joei Shikimoku** | The 1232 legal code reflecting Confucian values, replacing settlement of disputes by social connection |
| **Bushido** | Justice, courage, mercy, politeness, honesty, honour, loyalty and self-control; with no record before the mid-nineteenth century |
| **Noh drama** | Muromachi theatre of masks, art and poetry with increased Zen influence |
| **Sengoku period** | The Warring States, 1467–1568, a century-long civil war |
| **Kabuki** | Theatre developed in the 1600s: less refined, with less Buddhist influence, including comedy |

markdown:
# 12.1 The Rise of the Mongols

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The tribes

| Tribe | Description |
|---|---|
| Kharbag | A confederation of 38 clans; Temujin's group |
| Keraites | Turkish-Mongol Nestorian Christians |
| Tatars | Northeast of the Gobi Desert; opposed Temujin initially |
| Mergids | Kidnapped Temujin's wife; later defeated by Temujin and absorbed by the Kharbags |

## Temujin

The Mongols were nomadic. **Temujin**, later **Genghis Khan** — "Universal Ruler" — united the Mongol tribes. Mongol forces went on to conquer a vast empire stretching from the Pacific to Eastern Europe.

The basis was strict military discipline and the demand for absolute loyalty. They also learned the use of cannon from the Chinese and the Turks.

## Fighting techniques

The Mongols were accomplished horsemen and excellent with the short bow. Later they added battering rams, cannon, catapults, flaming arrows and gunpowder. From the Chinese they encountered the **fire-lance**, which evolved into more effective handguns and cannon by the end of the thirteenth century.

Two systems mattered as much as the weapons:

- The **yam system**: relay stations and messengers giving rapid communication
- Spies and informants, used to create maps of areas they intended to invade, combined with cavalry

Their units were the **arban**, the base unit of ten warriors, and the **tumen**, the largest unit, of ten thousand. Their signature tactic was the **feigned retreat**.

## Early campaigning

| Date | Campaign |
|---|---|
| 1207 | Defeated Xi Xia |
| Next | The Jin dynasty, using captured Chinese to help |
| 1219 | Conquered the Kara Khitai Empire and the Khwarazm Empire |

Artisans and scholars were captured rather than killed, which fits the pattern of Mongol rule described below.

## The empire of Chinggis Khan

The empire was diverse, and religions and cultures were tolerated by the Mongols. A script was derived for the Mongolian language. Chinggis Khan set up a capital at **Karakorum** and initially prohibited fellow Mongols from taking up sedentary occupations.

### Pax Mongolica

Under the **Pax Mongolica** trade routes were secured and monitored, and traders and goods were taxed. The Mongols were interested in collecting tribute from territory, and less interested in administering an empire — which explains why they left so much local government in place.

### Mongol rule

The Mongols were not usually oppressive rulers. They respected scholars, artists and artisans, and Confucians, Buddhists, Christians, Muslims, Jews and Zoroastrians were all welcomed at court.

## Trade and diplomacy

Chinese ports exported tea, silk, porcelain, precious stones, cotton and tropical products, with **Canton** a major port.

In 1245 Pope Innocent IV sent **John Plano Carpini** to the Mongol headquarters. Kuyuk Khan's reply to the Pope demanded submission and accused the Christians of attacking the Mongols.

## The death of an emperor

In 1226 the Khan took an army of 18,000 to complete the conquest of China. In 1227 Chinggis Khan died in battle, and his body was taken back to Karakorum.

The remaining land was divided four ways, between three sons and a grandson, and **Ogedai** became Great Khan, directing troops for conquest. The unified empire divided into several khanates:

- The Khanate of Kipchak, the **Golden Horde**
- The Khanate of **Chaghadai**
- The Khanate of Persia, the **Il-Khans**
- The **Great Khanate**

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Temujin / Genghis Khan** | "Universal Ruler"; the leader who united the Mongol tribes |
| **Fire-lance** | The Chinese military invention encountered by the Mongols, which evolved into handguns and cannon by the end of the thirteenth century |
| **Yam system** | Relay stations and messengers giving the Mongols rapid communication |
| **Arban** | The base Mongol unit of ten warriors |
| **Tumen** | The largest Mongol unit, of ten thousand |
| **Feigned retreat** | The Mongol tactic of pretending to retreat |
| **Karakorum** | The capital set up by Chinggis Khan |
| **Pax Mongolica** | The Mongol peace, under which trade routes were secured and monitored and traders and goods were taxed |
| **Khanates** | The divisions of the empire after Chinggis Khan's death: Kipchak (Golden Horde), Chaghadai, Persia (Il-Khans) and the Great Khanate |

title: The Khanates: Chagatai, the Golden Horde and the Ilkhanate
summary: Led by Chagatai Khan, son of Chinggis Khan. In the 1360s Tamerlane conquered its western half, and the khanate became increasingly decentralised into sub-khanates. Batu, Chinggis Khan's grandson, led
markdown:
# 12.2 The Khanates: Chagatai, the Golden Horde and the Ilkhanate

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The Chagatai Khanate, 1225–1687

Led by **Chagatai Khan**, son of Chinggis Khan. In the 1360s Tamerlane conquered its western half, and the khanate became increasingly decentralised into sub-khanates.

## The Golden Horde

**Batu**, Chinggis Khan's grandson, led the invasions of Russia — the only successful winter invasion of Russia in history. He also conquered Hungary, which had the most developed military at the time. The eventual goal was to conquer all of Europe.

Russia was divided into many little kingdoms and was unable to defend itself against invaders. In 1237–1238 Mongol forces invaded Russia, destroyed the cities that resisted, and took many others, including Kiev. They extended religious toleration to the Orthodox Church, and the guide is candid about the motive: there would have been problems if they had not.

### Effects on Russia

The Golden Horde increased Eurasian trade, acting as a conduit between Europe, the Middle East and Asia in honey, glassware, slaves, gunpowder, firearms, gems, textiles and rugs.

It also reshaped Russian society. High taxes on the peasants led peasants to give up land and crops to the aristocracy in exchange for protection from the Mongols, which is the origin of **serfdom**.

The conquest of Europe was interrupted by the death of Ogedai and the succession issues that followed. Russia, meanwhile, was isolated from West European influence, both commercial and cultural.

### Decline

The Golden Horde did not occupy or run the Russian government. It was a **tribute empire**: the Mongols forced the princes to pay taxes and tribute. Moscow's role was to collect the tribute, and when territories could not pay, the Muscovite princes took the territory over. The mechanism is worth holding on to, because it is self-reversing: the office of tax collector made Moscow steadily stronger while the Golden Horde declined. In 1380 at the **Battle of Kulikovo** the Russians defeated the Golden Horde.

## The Ilkhanate

**Hulegu** captured Baghdad and killed the Abbasid Empire. The Mongols then met the **Mamluks**, and Mongol expansion into North Africa was halted. Hulegu changed his plan to conquer the entire Muslim world.

Hulegu's cousin **Berke**, the new Khan of the Golden Horde, converted to Islam.

The Ilkhanate used local lords to administer taxes, tributes and census-taking. It was tolerant of scholars and artisans, assimilated Middle Eastern values, and some Mongols converted to Islam. It reinvigorated the Eurasian trade routes.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Chagatai Khan** | Son of Chinggis Khan and leader of the Chagatai Khanate, 1225–1687 |
| **Batu** | Chinggis Khan's grandson, who led the invasions of Russia and conquered Hungary |
| **Serfdom** | The arrangement by which peasants gave up land and crops to the aristocracy in exchange for protection from the Mongols |
| **Tribute empire** | The Golden Horde's method of rule: not occupying or running the Russian government, but forcing the princes to pay taxes and tribute |
| **Battle of Kulikovo** | The 1380 battle at which the Russians defeated the Golden Horde |
| **Hulegu** | The Mongol leader who captured Baghdad and ended the Abbasid Empire |
| **Berke** | Hulegu's cousin, new Khan of the Golden Horde, who converted to Islam |

markdown:
# 12.3 Yuan China and the Timurid Empire

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The Mongols in China

The Mongols succeeded the Song as rulers of China in the late thirteenth century. **Kublai Khan** toppled the last Song emperor in 1279.

### Keeping Mongols and Chinese apart

Kublai tried to prevent the Mongols from being absorbed into the Chinese. The highest government jobs were reserved for Mongols and other non-Chinese officials, though Chinese could still hold local positions, and there were no civil service examinations. Kublai was considered barbaric by many.

Culturally, Mongols and Chinese remained separate: the Mongols followed their own laws, and while some converted to Buddhism, most commoners kept their traditional religions.

### Expansion and openness

Yuan rulers under Kublai Khan expanded, sending Mongol armies into Vietnam and launching expeditions against the Malay kingdoms in Java and Sumatra.

Kublai turned **Khanbaliq**, that is Beijing, into a Chinese walled city, and welcomed foreigners into his court, among them Ibn Battuta and Marco Polo. Tolerance had practical results: the Pope sent Christian priests to Beijing, and Muslims set up communities in China. Chinese products moved towards Europe — gunpowder, porcelain and playing cards.

### Decline of the Yuan

Decline set in from the 1340s. The causes were excessive spending on conquests, tax issues, factionalism, corruption and natural disasters. The Yuan were replaced by the Ming dynasty in 1369.

## The Timurid Empire

**Timur the Lame**, or **Tamerlane**, was a Central Asian nomadic Turk. He was active during the decrease of Mongol power in Eurasia and wanted to restore the Mongol Empire.

His capital was **Samarkand**, famed for its architectural beauty. He moved armies into Persia, northwestern India and southern Russia. His campaign was the last nomadic incursion of its kind. He died in 1405.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Kublai Khan** | The Mongol ruler who toppled the last Song emperor in 1279 and founded Yuan rule in China |
| **Khanbaliq** | Beijing, which Kublai turned into a Chinese walled city |

# 13.1 The Byzantine Empire

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Justinian, 527–565

### The Nika Rebellion, 532

The Nika Rebellion nearly burned Constantinople, which was rebuilt in the aftermath. Its cause is instructive: the Greens and the Blues, ordinarily rivals, united in revolt against heavy taxation. The rebels besieged the palace, killed hundreds, burned a third of Constantinople, and crowned a new emperor in the Hippodrome.

### The Justinian Code and reconquest

Justinian issued the **Justinian Code** and reconquered most of the Mediterranean.

### Empress Theodora

Theodora was Justinian's wife, of scandalous origins and highly influential. Together with Justinian she built a strong economy based on taxes from the peasants.

### The Plague of Justinian, 541–549

The plague was caused by *Yersinia pestis*, the same bacterium responsible for the Black Death, and killed a fifth of the population of Constantinople. It was brought by infected rats in grain shipments from Egypt. Justinian's response was callous: there was no letup on taxes.

### Military exploits

Justinian fought Persians, Germans and others, and used taxation to fund a massive military. After Justinian the empire faced many diverse enemies and slowly lost territory for centuries.

## Politics

Emperors were the head and centre of elaborate court rituals. Beneath them sat a sophisticated, highly educated bureaucracy, and it was open to all classes. This bureaucracy helped organise the empire politically, socially and economically; provincial governors were appointed; and the state controlled the economy through the regulation of food prices, trade and silk production.

## Culture

Byzantine creativity appears in architecture, in richly coloured religious mosaics and in iconic paintings — a blend of Hellenistic tradition and Orthodoxy.

The empire heavily influenced Eastern Europe, both by missionaries and by conquest. **Cyril and Methodius** produced a new alphabet.

## Religious tension

Byzantine emperors traditionally appointed the **Patriarch**, the highest church official in Constantinople. There were significant differences in clergy culture and rights, and disagreements with the Pope. In 1054 came the **Great Schism**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Nika Rebellion** | The 532 revolt in which the Greens and Blues united against heavy taxation, burning a third of Constantinople and crowning a new emperor in the Hippodrome |
| **Justinian Code** | The legal code issued by Justinian |
| **Theodora** | Justinian's wife, of scandalous origins and highly influential, who with him built an economy based on taxes from peasants |
| **Plague of Justinian** | The epidemic of 541–549, caused by *Yersinia pestis*, which killed a fifth of the population of Constantinople, brought by infected rats in grain shipments from Egypt |
| **Cyril and Methodius** | The missionaries who produced a new alphabet, part of Byzantine influence on Eastern Europe |
| **Patriarch** | The highest church official in Constantinople, traditionally appointed by the emperor |
| **Great Schism** | The split of 1054 between the Byzantine church and the Pope |

markdown:
# 13.2 Crisis in the Fourteenth Century: Famine, War and the Black Death

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Early problems

The century opens with the **Great Famine** of 1315–1317.

## The Hundred Years' War

### Causes

In 1328 Charles IV of France died with no heirs and no brothers, and his closest male relative was King Edward III of England. To that dynastic problem the guide adds pressure from the Great Famine and tension between the French and English royal families. The war was an intermittent conflict with multiple phases.

### Effects

- Nascent nationalism, and national heroes: Edward the Black Prince, Joan of Arc
- The end of English land claims in France
- A revival of chivalry
- The beginning of gunpowder in European warfare
- The beginning of standing, professionalised militaries
- Diplomacy and intelligence

## The Black Death

The Black Death was the most devastating plague in European history, and the first epidemic since the sixth century. It was spread by merchants on the trade routes, by fleas on rats. Up to fifty per cent of all Europeans died, and the population fell from 75 million to 35 million. There were mass graves instead of individual coffins.

### Treatment

Medieval treatment aimed to balance the four humours — yellow bile, black bile, blood and phlegm. Understanding that aim is what makes the remedies intelligible, if not effective.

| Ineffective treatments | Mildly effective treatments |
|---|---|
| Self-flagellation — whipping yourself | Quarantine |
| Drinking the pus of lanced buboes | Isolation and plague hospitals |
| Grinding an emerald and drinking it in wine | Bathing with vinegar and rosewater |
| A mixture of Armenian clay, precious metals, aloe, myrrh and saffron | Drinking a mixture of vinegar, cider, spices, rosemary and wormwood |
| Roasting the shells of fresh eggs, grinding them, adding marigolds and treacle, and drinking it in warm beer | |
| Placing a hen in the swellings | |
| Drinking urine twice a day | |

The effective column has one thing in common that the ineffective column lacks: it separates the sick from the well, or cleans, rather than trying to rebalance the body.

### Impacts

- Persecution: Jews, foreigners, the poor and pilgrims were all blamed for the plague
- De-urbanisation, as cities declined
- Rapid depopulation, bringing inflation and a lack of food and supplies
- A loss of faith, with God and the church blamed and hope lost
- A breakdown of societal structure, including the end of the lord–vassal system and of feudalism
- Lawlessness and panic
- An increase in medicine and medical practices
- Opportunity for wealth gain and better working conditions, which led to revolts such as the Peasants' Revolt of 1381
- A "correction" of overpopulation, as the guide puts it with a question mark

Notice that the last two run against the others: the same depopulation that broke the social order also gave the survivors bargaining power.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Great Famine** | The famine of 1315–1317 |
| **Hundred Years' War** | The intermittent conflict beginning after the death of Charles IV of France in 1328, whose closest male relative was Edward III of England |
| **Black Death** | The most devastating plague in European history, the first epidemic since the sixth century, spread by merchants on trade routes through fleas on rats; up to 50 per cent of Europeans died |
| **The four humours** | Yellow bile, black bile, blood and phlegm, which medieval treatment sought to balance |
| **Peasants' Revolt** | The revolt of 1381, arising from the post-plague opportunity for wealth gain and better working conditions |

markdown:
# 13.3 The Renaissance in Italy

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

People in Italy between 1350 and 1550 saw themselves as a rebirth of Classical antiquity, and called the period the **Renaissance**, French for "rebirth". The name is a claim about themselves, not a label applied later.

## The intellectual Renaissance: humanism and secularism

**Renaissance humanism** was an intellectual movement. Humanists studied the liberal arts based on Greek and Roman authors, emphasising rhetoric, poetry and moral philosophy.

**Petrarch** (1304–1374) is the "father of the Italian Renaissance". Humanism promoted Latin and took an interest in Classical Greece.

In **Florence**, humanists focused on leading an active life, and the city council members believed that intellectual life was for citizens — which is why Florentine humanism has a civic character rather than a monastic one.

Women's participation in the Renaissance varied. Some upper-class women received an education and contributed to intellectual life.

## The artistic Renaissance

**Masaccio**'s *Tribute Money* in the Brancacci Chapel is considered the first great work of Early Renaissance art. It introduced a realistic art style with rational perspective.

### Architecture

Renaissance architects were inspired by Roman architectural models. Interiors used Classical columns, rounded arches and coffered ceilings that balanced proportion and did not overwhelm worshippers.

### The masters

| Artist | Work and significance |
|---|---|
| **Leonardo da Vinci** | *The Last Supper* represents the High Renaissance concern for idealising nature. He used gesture and movement to depict character and inner nature; his experimental technique caused the fresco to deteriorate |
| **Raphael** | *School of Athens*, painted 1510–1511 in the Vatican, depicts an imaginary gathering of ancient philosophers, with Plato and Aristotle at the centre |
| **Michelangelo** | Dedicated to art; the *David* statue |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Renaissance** | French for "rebirth"; the name Italians of 1350–1550 gave their own age, seeing themselves as a rebirth of Classical antiquity |
| **Renaissance humanism** | The intellectual movement that studied the liberal arts based on Greek and Roman authors, emphasising rhetoric, poetry and moral philosophy |
| **Petrarch** | 1304–1374; the "father of the Italian Renaissance" |
| **Masaccio** | Painter of *Tribute Money*, considered the first great work of Early Renaissance art, which introduced a realistic style with rational perspective |

# 13.4 Europe's Political Landscape in the Fifteenth Century

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## State-building

In the second half of the fifteenth century, the monarchies in France, Spain and England were building modern states.

## The Italian states

Five major powers emerged.

| State | Form |
|---|---|
| Milan | A duchy |
| Florence | A republic |
| Venice | A republic |
| The Papal States | — |
| The Kingdom of Naples | — |

### Boundaries and conflict

The political boundaries in Europe at this time help explain the frequent wars between France and the Holy Roman Empire.

Despite becoming wealthy, the Italian states were not strong, and the two facts together produced the outcome: from 1494 Italy was a battlefield in the power struggle between the French and Spanish monarchies, leading to Spanish domination in the sixteenth century.

**Niccolò Machiavelli** (1469–1527) wrote *The Prince* (1513), an influential work on political power.

## Western Europe

### France

The Hundred Years' War left France prosperous but with a sense of national feeling. King **Louis XI** (1461–1483) strengthened the monarchy by subduing the great lords and creating a strong financial base through taxation.

### England

For England the Hundred Years' War caused financial strain and losses.

### Spain

Spain experienced the growth of a strong national monarchy by the end of the fifteenth century. The marriage of **Isabella of Castile** (1474–1504) and **Ferdinand of Aragon** (1479–1516) in 1469 was its foundation. They filled the royal council with middle-class officials and reorganised the administration of government and the military.

## Central and Eastern Europe

The **Holy Roman Empire** failed to develop strong monarchical authority. The house of **Habsburg** became an important political power, and Austria played a role in European affairs.

In Eastern Europe, rulers struggled to achieve centralisation of their territory, often facing challenges from different religious groups such as Catholics and Eastern Orthodox Christians.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Niccolò Machiavelli** | 1469–1527; author of *The Prince* (1513), an influential work on political power |
| **Louis XI** | King of France 1461–1483, who strengthened the monarchy by subduing the great lords and building a financial base through taxation |
| **Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon** | Rulers whose 1469 marriage founded a strong Spanish national monarchy; they filled the royal council with middle-class officials and reorganised government and the military |
| **Habsburg** | The house that became an important political power in the Holy Roman Empire, with Austria playing a role in European affairs |

# 13.5 Renaissances Beyond Europe

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

This lesson covers material the guide marks as supplementary. Its purpose is comparative: a revival of arts and learning under wealthy patrons is not a uniquely European event.

## The Timurid Renaissance

The **Timurid Empire** was a Turko-Mongol empire founded by Timur, or Tamerlane, in 1370. It saw a revival of arts and sciences that spread across the Muslim world and rivalled the achievements of the Renaissance in Europe.

### Persian seven-coloured tiles

Persian **Haft Rang** tiles were highly decorative, glazed tiles used to adorn the exteriors and interiors of both secular and religious buildings, showing plants, birds, people and calligraphy. Artists could create mosaics by painting directly onto the tiles, which made the process less expensive and more efficient than assembling one from cut pieces.

### The Herat school

The **Herat school** was a fifteenth-century style of Persian miniature painting, produced under the patronage of the Timurid rulers.

### Poetry

**Hafiz** and **Jami**, both supported by Timur's patronage, and both Sufi Muslims.

## Japan's Renaissance: the Muromachi period

**Karamono** were the artistic and cultural products of China, traditionally highly prized in Japan. Members of the Ashikaga clan, who ruled the country as shogun, amassed a huge collection of karamono at their mansion.

Japanese paintings incorporated Zen aspects, such as gratitude for beauty and nature, and Zen Buddhist monks moved from Japan to Ming China to study authentic Chinese paintings.

**Josetsu** is the father of Japanese ink painting. His *Catching a Fish With a Gourd* is a piece of Zen humour, a **koan** or riddle in visual form, designed to provoke the viewer into new ways of seeing.

**Ryoanji** temple in north Kyoto is affiliated with a branch of Zen Buddhism, which pursued enlightenment or awakening through personal experience and meditation. It was a great Zen centre for the cultural activities of the elite, under the patronage of the Hosokawa family.

**Haiku** is a short poetic form of 5-7-5 syllables.

## The Benin Renaissance

The **Benin Bronzes** are a group of more than a thousand metal plaques and sculptures that decorated the royal palaces of the Kingdom of Benin in modern-day Nigeria. The bronzes celebrate Benin's great kings and military victories, and include warrior figures, masks and animal figures.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Timurid Empire** | The Turko-Mongol empire founded by Timur in 1370, whose revival of arts and sciences rivalled the European Renaissance |
| **Haft Rang** | Persian seven-coloured tiles, highly decorative and glazed, painted directly to make mosaics more cheaply and efficiently |
| **Herat school** | The fifteenth-century style of Persian miniature painting under Timurid patronage |
| **Karamono** | The artistic and cultural products of China, traditionally highly prized in Japan |
| **Josetsu** | The father of Japanese ink painting, author of *Catching a Fish With a Gourd* |
| **Koan** | A riddle, here in visual form, designed to provoke the viewer into new ways of seeing |
| **Haiku** | A short poetic form of 5-7-5 syllables |
| **Benin Bronzes** | More than a thousand metal plaques and sculptures decorating the royal palaces of the Kingdom of Benin, celebrating its kings and military victories |

markdown:
# 14.1 An Age of Exploration and Expansion

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Europeans were not first

Europeans were not the first in the Asian trade; Indian Ocean trade had thrived for centuries. Vasco da Gama's voyage to India in the late fifteenth century is seen as a key moment, but Asian and African trade networks were already well established. The Portuguese kept the route secret until the Dutch later discovered it.

Muslim merchants had long dominated the spice trade, with trade routes connecting various regions.

## Islam and the spice trade

Muslim merchants had been involved in the spice trade for centuries, sailing from ports in Asia. By the thirteenth century Islam had a presence in the Southeast Asian islands and was spreading inland. That spread was also driven by new sultanates, such as **Malacca**, founded in the early fifteenth century.

## The spread of Islam in West Africa

Muslim commercial and religious influence spread south across the Sahara to the Niger River valley. Muslim traders — Arabs and local converts — brought Islamic values, culture and legal traditions, and this contributed to state formation, for example the kingdom of **Mali**. Trade and state-building here are the same process.

### Timbuktu

**Timbuktu** became a major commercial hub for the trans-Saharan trade, dealing in gold, salt and other goods. It had a well-developed social and economic system, with a significant Islamic scholarly community. **Leo Africanus** described its wealth, including its trade in precious goods and its use of currency such as cowrie shells and gold.

## Motives for European expansion

The motives are summarised as **"God, Gold, and Glory"**:

- Missionary efforts to spread Christianity
- The desire for wealth — gold and spices
- The pursuit of fame and national glory

To these must be added the means as well as the motive: technological advances such as better ships and navigational tools including the compass and the astrolabe enabled these voyages.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Malacca** | A sultanate founded in the early fifteenth century that helped spread Islam in Southeast Asia |
| **Mali** | A West African kingdom whose formation was contributed to by Muslim traders bringing Islamic values, culture and legal traditions |
| **Timbuktu** | Major commercial hub of the trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt, with a significant Islamic scholarly community |
| **Leo Africanus** | The writer who described Timbuktu's wealth, including its use of cowrie shells and gold as currency |
| **"God, Gold, and Glory"** | The three motives for European expansion: spreading Christianity, wealth, and fame and national glory |
| **Astrolabe** | A navigational tool which, with the compass and better ships, enabled the voyages |

# 14.2 The Portuguese Maritime Empire

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The start of Portuguese exploration

Portugal began exploring the western coast of Africa under **Prince Henry the Navigator**, with three aims: the gold trade, weakening Muslim states, and spreading Christianity. Portugal established a school for navigators and built forts along the African coast.

## Voyages to India

**Vasco da Gama**'s voyage to India in 1497–1499 was a milestone. He reached the port of **Calicut**, and his voyage was sponsored in order to break the Muslim monopoly on the spice trade.

Subsequent Portuguese efforts included establishing trade posts and forts, such as at **Malacca**, to control trade routes. The pattern is a maritime empire of ports and forts, not of territory.

## Success and its limits

Portugal succeeded initially because of a strong navy, advanced ships and cannon technology.

It then faced challenges from Muslim rivals and later from European competitors such as Spain, England and the Netherlands, and struggled to maintain dominance in the long term because of over-extension, high costs and competition. The same thin network of forts that made rapid success possible was what made it expensive to hold.

## Dividing up the spoils of exploration

Portugal and Spain signed the **Treaty of Tordesillas** in 1494 to divide the newly discovered territories. The treaty set a **line of demarcation**, giving most of the Americas to Spain and areas east — including Africa and Asia — to Portugal. Disputes later arose over the exact boundaries, and this led to several violations of the treaty in the future.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Prince Henry the Navigator** | The Portuguese prince under whom exploration of the western coast of Africa began, aiming at gold, weakening Muslim states and spreading Christianity |
| **Vasco da Gama** | Explorer whose 1497–1499 voyage reached Calicut, sponsored to break the Muslim monopoly on the spice trade |
| **Treaty of Tordesillas** | The 1494 agreement between Portugal and Spain dividing newly discovered territories |
| **Line of demarcation** | The line set by the treaty, giving most of the Americas to Spain and areas east, including Africa and Asia, to Portugal |

title: The Conquest of the "New World"
summary: Christopher Columbus, an Italian sailing for Spain, reached the Americas in 1492, mistakenly believing he had reached Asia. Spanish conquistadors — Hernán Cortés in Mexico and Francisco Pizarro in Per
markdown:
# 14.3 The Conquest of the "New World"

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Spanish exploration and conquest

**Christopher Columbus**, an Italian sailing for Spain, reached the Americas in 1492, mistakenly believing he had reached Asia.

Spanish **conquistadors** — **Hernán Cortés** in Mexico and **Francisco Pizarro** in Peru — conquered major indigenous empires, the Aztec and the Inca. Three things made this possible: superior weapons, alliances with rival groups, and the spread of European diseases. Spain established a large colonial empire in the Americas, including Mexico, Central America and much of South America.

## The Portuguese in Brazil

The Portuguese explorer **Pedro Cabral** accidentally discovered Brazil in 1500. Portugal established colonies there, initially focusing on extracting gold and silver, and later on plantation-based agriculture in sugar and coffee. It developed a colonial administration system and a multiracial society, with European, indigenous and African influences.

## Governing the empires

Spain and Portugal constructed colonial empires with administrative systems. Spain's included **viceroyalties**, such as New Spain and Peru, to govern large territories; Portugal developed a colonial administration in Brazil.

Latin America became a multiracial society, with **mestizos** — of mixed European and indigenous descent — and other mixed-race groups emerging through intermarriage and African slavery. Social status was calculated by ancestry: the closer to pure European blood you were, the higher your social status.

The **Catholic Church** played a major role in colonising efforts, converting indigenous peoples, building missions and influencing social and cultural life.

## Exploiting the riches

Europeans exploited the Americas' natural resources, especially gold and silver. Mines in Mexico, Peru and Bolivia were major sources, and precious metals were shipped to Europe, fuelling economic growth there.

The **encomienda system** was instituted, under which European settlers received land and indigenous labour. Its stated main purpose was to convert indigenous people to Christianity; its effect was the exploitation and abuse of the indigenous population.

African slaves were then brought to the Americas to work on plantations of sugar, tobacco and similar crops, as indigenous populations were decimated by disease and overwork.

## Opposing viewpoints on European exploration

| Position | Representative | Argument |
|---|---|---|
| Approval | Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo | European exploration was a "march of civilisation", bringing Christianity and progress |
| Condemnation | Bartolomé de Las Casas | Condemned the brutal treatment of indigenous peoples and the atrocities committed by conquistadors |

## Competition intensifies

Other European powers — the English, Dutch and French — entered the competition for American colonies and trade. They established settlements, traded, and competed for resources in the Caribbean and North America.

## The Columbian Exchange

The **Columbian Exchange** was the transfer of plants, animals, diseases and cultures between the Americas and the Old World. It had positive effects, such as new crops and increased food production, and negative ones, such as the spread of disease and indigenous population decline.

The asymmetry of the disease exchange has an explanation worth stating: the Europeans did not suffer in the same way as the indigenous peoples because the indigenous peoples had not had plagues, being too separated from one another.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Conquistadors** | Spanish conquerors such as Cortés in Mexico and Pizarro in Peru, who defeated the Aztec and Inca empires with superior weapons, alliances with rival groups and European diseases |
| **Pedro Cabral** | The Portuguese explorer who accidentally discovered Brazil in 1500 |
| **Viceroyalty** | A Spanish administrative division, such as New Spain or Peru, governing large territories |
| **Mestizo** | A person of mixed European and indigenous descent |
| **Encomienda system** | The system granting European settlers land and indigenous labour, whose main stated purpose was to convert indigenous people to Christianity, and which led to exploitation and abuse |
| **Columbian Exchange** | The transfer of plants, animals, diseases and cultures between the Americas and the Old World |

markdown:
# 14.4 Africa in Transition

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The Portuguese in Africa

The Portuguese initially aimed to find a sea route to the Spice Islands, but also engaged in trade along the African coast, focusing on gold and later on slaves. They seized East African port cities — **Kilwa**, **Sofala**, **Mombasa** — and built forts to control trade, especially in gold.

## The slave trade

European exploration of the African coast led to a significant increase in the slave trade from the sixteenth to the eighteenth centuries. Enslaved Africans were forcibly removed from their homes and exported to plantations in the Americas, usually cash-crop plantations of cotton, tobacco and sugarcane.

Slavery existed in Africa before European involvement, but the transatlantic slave trade expanded its scale and brutality. The Dutch, English and French also became involved in the West African slave trade, competing with the Portuguese.

### Impact

The transatlantic slave trade devastated African societies, displacing millions and disrupting economies. European merchants, local elites and African intermediaries all participated, often destabilising kingdoms such as **Kongo**. The trade was characterised by high mortality rates on the **Middle Passage**, the voyage from Africa to the Americas, and by brutal conditions in the Americas.

## European settlement in Africa

The Dutch were the first Europeans to settle in South Africa, establishing a colony at the **Cape of Good Hope** as a supply station. The colony evolved, with Dutch farmers, the **Boers**, and other European settlers, and later came into conflict with indigenous groups such as the Bantu-speaking peoples over land and resources.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Kilwa, Sofala, Mombasa** | East African port cities seized by the Portuguese, who built forts to control trade, especially in gold |
| **Middle Passage** | The voyage from Africa to the Americas, characterised by high mortality rates |
| **Kongo** | An example of a kingdom destabilised by the slave trade |
| **Cape of Good Hope** | The site of the first European settlement in South Africa, a Dutch supply station |
| **Boers** | Dutch farmers in the South African colony, who later came into conflict with indigenous groups over land and resources |

# 14.5 Southeast Asia in the Era of the Spice Trade

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## European competition

The Portuguese, Dutch, English and French competed for control of the spice trade, targeting **Malacca** and other key ports. The **Dutch East India Company**, the VOC, emerged dominant, pushing out its rivals and controlling the trade routes.

## Society and culture in precolonial Southeast Asia

Southeast Asian societies, such as **Siam** and Malacca, balanced local traditions with new influences, including Islam and Buddhism. Both religions shaped political structures, while trade in spices and textiles drove economic growth.

The European presence remained limited initially, but grew, affecting local politics and culture over time. It is worth being precise about that sequence: Europeans entered a functioning regional system as competitors within it before they dominated it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Malacca** | A key port targeted by European powers competing for the spice trade |
| **Dutch East India Company (VOC)** | The company that emerged dominant in Southeast Asia, pushing out rivals and controlling trade routes |
| **Siam** | A Southeast Asian society that balanced local traditions with new influences including Islam and Buddhism |

markdown:
# 15.1 The Protestant Reformation

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Europe around 1500

The Reformation happens in a Europe with a particular political shape, and the shape matters, because whether a reformer survived depended on who ruled his territory.

| Region | Situation |
|---|---|
| Spain | The Reconquista finished by the kingdoms of Aragon and Castile — Spain, but two separate kingdoms |
| Italy | The Italian city-states and their trade |
| France | Politically unified and stable under the House of Valois since the end of the Hundred Years' War |
| The Holy Roman Empire | Somewhat decentralised, ruled by Maximilian I, founder of the Habsburg dynasty. Effectively hereditary, though the emperors still had to be elected. Joanna of Aragon and Castile married Philip the Handsome of Austria |
| England | Stabilised under the Tudors, under Henry |

The Ottoman Empire was rising in the East.

## The church in the 1500s

Grievances against the church were as much financial as doctrinal:

- Popes meddled in political and secular affairs
- Extreme wealth, and **indulgences**
- Increased fees for marriages and baptisms
- Some citizens felt squeezed, and desired a simpler church
- Resentment of clerical privileges and immunities

## Martin Luther

**Martin Luther** was initially not opposed to the church. In 1517 he wrote the **95 Theses**, arguing that the church could not save you from purgatory. In 1521 he was excommunicated and outlawed, but was protected by Prince Frederick III, and he still gained the support of the people. In 1522 came the publication of his German translation of the New Testament, and in 1526 an English translation.

### Zwingli

**Ulrich Zwingli** (1484–1531) was similar to Luther and based in Zurich. For him scripture was the sole basis of religious truth, and he attacked indulgences, the Mass, monasticism and clerical celibacy.

## The core of Protestantism

- **Salvation by faith alone**: if you believe in God, you will go to heaven
- The **priesthood of all believers**: this stressed the critical importance of the Bible and the claim that everyone could interpret it, which weakens the authority of the church
- A general rejection of elaborate church rituals

## The Reformation spreads

**John Calvin** established a Protestant theocracy in Geneva around 1541. Calvinism spread through parts of France and Scotland. Some Calvinists in Scotland, and eventually in England, became known as **Puritans**; in France they were the **Huguenots**.

Calvinists were not popular, which is directly relevant to the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre. Calvinist practices were very strict and limiting — people were not allowed to dance, for example.

## Comparing the three churches

| | Catholicism | Lutheranism | Calvinism |
|---|---|---|---|
| Salvation | Through faith and good works | Through faith | God predetermines who will be saved |
| Sacraments | Seven rituals: baptism, confirmation, marriage, ordination, communion, anointing the sick and repentance | Accepts some but rejects others; rituals cannot erase sin, only God can | Accepts some but rejects others; rituals cannot erase sin, only God can |
| Head | The Pope | Ministers | Council of Elders |
| Bible | One source of truth, with church tradition as well | The only source of truth | The only source of truth |
| How belief is revealed | Priests interpret the Bible and church teachings | People read and interpret themselves | People read and interpret themselves |

## The Anglican Church

**Henry VIII** was a Catholic, but his annulment was denied, and he established a church that would allow the divorce. The sequence runs:

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 1534 | The Act of Supremacy |
| 1535–1539 | Dissolution and destruction of the monasteries |
| — | Henry died leaving Edward VI, a child |
| — | Mary I of Scotland seized the throne, a staunch Catholic, bringing fears of religious violence and persecution |
| 1558–1559 | Elizabeth I revised the Act of Supremacy in 1559, calming tensions; Protestant |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Indulgences** | A source of the church's extreme wealth and a target of reformers' attacks |
| **95 Theses** | Luther's 1517 document, arguing that the church could not save you from purgatory |
| **Ulrich Zwingli** | 1484–1531, based in Zurich; held scripture to be the sole basis of religious truth and attacked indulgences, the Mass, monasticism and clerical celibacy |
| **Salvation by faith alone** | The Protestant doctrine that if you believe in God, you will go to heaven |
| **Priesthood of all believers** | The doctrine that everyone could interpret the Bible, which weakens the authority of the church |
| **John Calvin** | Established a Protestant theocracy in Geneva around 1541 |
| **Puritans** | Calvinists in Scotland and eventually England |
| **Huguenots** | Calvinists in France |
| **Act of Supremacy** | The 1534 act establishing the Anglican Church, revised by Elizabeth I in 1559 |
